templates.title: Payment method mix per business category and month, split tenders counted per tender
templates.subtopic: a complete category × month × method grid, LEFT JOIN zeros, local-time months, ratio of totals

sections.scenario: A point-of-sale product lets a seller take a payment in several tenders: a customer pays part in cash and the rest by card, or two friends split a bill across two cards. Each tender records how it was taken: contactless (tap), chip (dip), swipe, keyed-in (the card number typed by hand) or cash. A product team wants a monthly view of the payment method mix for each business category, to see how fast tap is replacing chip and swipe and where keyed-in payments are still common, measured both by number of tenders and by money.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns business_category, month, method, tenders, amount_cents, tender_share, amount_share, ordered by business_category, month, method. A category-month is a seller's business_category with a month; {{month_rule}} Each tender counts once, under its own method — a payment split across two tenders contributes two tenders. {{status_rule}} {{change_rule}} For every category-month with at least one counted tender, return one row for each of the five methods in tender_methods, including methods with no tenders (0, 0, 0, 0). tenders counts the method's tenders, amount_cents sums their amounts, tender_share is tenders over all counted tenders of the category-month, and amount_share is amount_cents over all counted cents of the category-month, both rounded to 4 decimal places.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Money stays in integer cents until the division. The sample has {{payments}} payments and {{tenders}} tender rows.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical sellers, categories, amounts and schema. The five method names are this exercise's simplification of how card-present payments are taken. No individual buyer appears anywhere; the report is per category.
sections.criteria: One row per counted tender, never per payment; only COMPLETED tenders; the month in the stated time zone (the seller's own zone at Hard+); cash tendered minus change (Very Hard); a complete five-method grid with zeros; shares as ratios of totals with numeric division and correct rounding; deterministic order; can discuss per-payment definitions, dominance by large sellers and incremental aggregation.

clarifications.q: A payment is half cash, half chip. How does it count?
clarifications.a: As one cash tender and one chip tender, each with its own amount.

clarifications.q: Which time zone decides the month?
clarifications.a: {{month_rule}}

clarifications.q: A category-month has no keyed-in tenders. Does it still get a keyed row?
clarifications.a: Yes, with zeros. Every category-month with counted tenders has exactly five rows.

clarifications.q: Is amount_share the average of each payment's share?
clarifications.a: No. It is the method's cents over the category-month's cents: a ratio of totals.

clarifications.q: How is rounding done?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of the exact ratio, half away from zero.

hints: Build one row per counted tender first, with its category, month, method and amount; everything after aggregates that.
The grid is the category-months that exist × tender_methods; LEFT JOIN the counted tenders onto it and count a column from the right side, so empty cells count 0.
Compute each category-month's totals once (a CTE or a window SUM(…) OVER (PARTITION BY category, month)) and divide numerics, not integers.
followups: Product wants the same mix by payment rather than by tender: "share of payments that used any contactless tender". Write the definition precisely and say how a split payment counts.
A large seller in one category takes most of the payments. How would you show the mix per seller so one seller does not dominate the category, and what would you have to suppress for small sellers?
The tender table grows by hundreds of millions of rows a month. What would you pre-aggregate daily, and how do late corrections (a tender marked failed hours later) reach the monthly numbers?
Each seller's time zone can change when they move a location. Which zone should an old payment use, and how would you store it so the report never changes retroactively?

rules.ask: The spec counts tenders, not payments. What does counting distinct payments do to a half-cash, half-card sale, and to the two shares?
Where does a category-month with no keyed-in tenders get its keyed row with zeros in your query?
A seller in Los Angeles takes a payment at 18:00 local on 31 January. Which month does your query put it in, and which month does the seller see on their own reports?
Is the method's share the average of per-payment shares or the ratio of totals? Show a case where they differ.
A customer hands over 20.00 in cash for a 13.50 remainder. Which amount does your query add up, and which one is the money the seller kept?

templates.title: Offline-mode payments: hours until forwarded and the share declined once forwarded
templates.subtopic: first qualifying event per entity (DISTINCT ON or ROW_NUMBER), LEFT JOIN with a window condition, NULL-safe averages

sections.scenario: A point-of-sale app can take card payments while the device has no internet connection (offline mode): the payment is stored on the device and forwarded for processing when the connection returns. Until then the seller does not know whether it will be approved, so a payment forwarded late, or declined once forwarded, is money the seller may not receive. A product team wants a monthly report per seller: how long offline payments waited before they were forwarded, how many were declined once forwarded, and — listed apart, because they are a different problem — the payments that were never forwarded at all.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns seller_id, month, offline_payments, forwarded, avg_hours_to_forward, declined_share, never_forwarded, never_forwarded_cents: one row per seller and month with at least one offline payment, ordered by seller_id, month. month is the first day of the UTC month of taken_at (the month the payment was taken, not the month it was forwarded). {{attempt_rule}} {{window_rule}} A payment is forwarded if it has a first decisive attempt that the window rule (if any) does not exclude; otherwise it is never forwarded. avg_hours_to_forward is the average, over forwarded payments, of the hours from taken_at to the first decisive attempt, rounded to 2 decimal places; declined_share is the share of forwarded payments whose first decisive attempt was DECLINED, rounded to 4 decimal places; both are NULL when nothing was forwarded. never_forwarded and never_forwarded_cents count those payments and sum their amount_cents (0 when there are none); they never enter the average or the share.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Every seller-month with an offline payment appears, even one where nothing was forwarded. The sample has {{payments}} offline payments and {{attempts}} forward attempts.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical sellers, amounts, delays and schema. How long a real device may hold offline payments, and what happens to them afterwards, is set by the product's own published rules; check current docs. No buyer data is used.
sections.criteria: The first decisive attempt per payment with a deterministic tie-break; ERROR attempts ignored; later attempts ignored; the forwarding window applied inclusively with late payments moved to never forwarded (Very Hard); grouped by the month the payment was taken; NULL average and share when nothing was forwarded; never-forwarded counts and cents kept apart from the averages; correct rounding and order; can discuss alerts, percentiles and late data.

clarifications.q: A payment taken on 31 August and forwarded on 1 September. Which month?
clarifications.a: August: the month of taken_at.

clarifications.q: What makes an attempt decisive?
clarifications.a: Its result is APPROVED or DECLINED. An ERROR attempt settled nothing.

clarifications.q: Two attempts have the same attempted_at.
clarifications.a: The lower attempt_id comes first.

clarifications.q: A seller-month where every payment is still unforwarded.
clarifications.a: It appears with forwarded = 0 and NULL for the average and the share.

clarifications.q: How are the hours computed?
clarifications.a: The exact interval in seconds divided by 3600, averaged, then ROUND(…, 2).

hints: Pick each payment's first decisive attempt on its own (DISTINCT ON (payment_id) … ORDER BY payment_id, attempted_at, attempt_id, or ROW_NUMBER) before joining it to the payments.
LEFT JOIN that onto offline_payments so unforwarded payments stay; any condition that can make a payment "not forwarded" belongs in the join, not in a WHERE.
AVG and COUNT(column) ignore NULLs; NULLIF(…, 0) keeps a division by zero from failing.
followups: Sellers want to be warned while it still matters. Turn this monthly report into a live alert: which payments would you flag, when, and from what data on the device?
The average hides a long tail. Which percentile would you report instead, and how would you compute it per seller-month in SQL?
Forward attempts arrive from devices hours late and sometimes twice. How do you keep this report correct as they trickle in, and when is a month final?
A product manager reads a high decline share as "offline mode is risky for these sellers". What else could explain it, and what would you check before anyone draws that conclusion?

rules.ask: A payment was declined, then a retry was approved an hour later. Which attempt settles it in this report, and why does using the latest one change the decline share?
Where do payments with no decisive attempt go in your query, and how do they reach never_forwarded?
Which month does a payment taken on 31 August and forwarded on 1 September land in, and why does the report use the month it was taken?
A payment has three ERROR attempts and nothing else. What does your query report for it?
Which denominator does your decline share use, and what happens to it when half the payments were never forwarded?

templates.title: Instalment schedules: on-time plans per purchase-month cohort, and late instalments by number
templates.subtopic: running totals on two sides matched by threshold, cohort aggregation, dates versus timestamps

sections.scenario: A buy-now-pay-later product splits a purchase into four instalments: the first is paid at checkout and the rest fall due every two weeks. A team that reports on repayment behaviour wants, for each month's purchases (a cohort), the share of plans in which every instalment was paid by its due date, and how many instalments were paid late, broken down by instalment number. The report is about the product's schedule design, not about any person: no conclusion about an individual customer's credit is drawn from it.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns cohort_month, plans, on_time_plans, on_time_share, late_2, late_3, late_4, unpaid_instalments, one row per cohort, ordered by cohort_month. A plan's cohort is the first day of the UTC month of purchased_at. This exercise's rule (check current docs for any real product's terms): payments are applied in paid_at, payment_id order to the plan's earliest instalment that is not yet fully paid; instalment k is fully paid by the payment that brings the plan's running total of payments to at least the sum of instalments 1 to k. {{payment_rule}} An instalment is on time if the UTC date of the payment that fully paid it is on or before its due_date, late if after, and unpaid if no payment fully paid it. plans counts the cohort's plans; on_time_plans counts plans whose four instalments were all on time; on_time_share = on_time_plans / plans rounded to 4 decimal places; late_2, late_3 and late_4 count late instalments with that number; unpaid_instalments counts unpaid instalments of any number.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Every instalment in the sample was already due when the data was extracted, and no plan was paid more than its amount. The sample has {{plans}} plans and {{payments}} payments.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical plans, amounts and payment behaviour. The four-instalment, two-weekly schedule, the order in which payments are applied and the on-time rule are this exercise's rules. Late fees, refunds and rescheduling are out of scope here. The report is aggregated per cohort and draws no legal, credit-worthiness or eligibility conclusion about any person.
sections.criteria: Payments applied in order with running totals rather than matched one-to-one; an instalment judged by the payment that completes it; UTC date compared with the due date, not a timestamp; unpaid instalments make a plan not on time and are counted separately; per-plan then per-cohort aggregation with correct rounding; pay-ahead payments completing several instalments (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss incomplete cohorts, grace periods and refunds, and keeps the report free of conclusions about individuals.

clarifications.q: A payment arrives at 23:59 UTC on the due date.
clarifications.a: On time: compare the payment's UTC date with due_date.

clarifications.q: A customer pays half an instalment before the due date and the rest after.
clarifications.a: Late: the instalment is judged by the payment that completes it.

clarifications.q: A plan has an unpaid instalment and nothing late. Is it an on-time plan?
clarifications.a: No. Every instalment must have been fully paid by its due date.

clarifications.q: Does a payment say which instalment it is for?
clarifications.a: No. Payments are applied to the earliest instalment not yet fully paid, so the running totals decide.

clarifications.q: Can instalment 1 be late?
clarifications.a: It is paid at checkout, on its due date, so it never is; the output has no late_1 column.

hints: Two running totals per plan: the cumulative amount due through each instalment, and the cumulative amount paid through each payment (SUM(…) OVER (PARTITION BY plan_id ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id)).
Instalment k is fully paid at the earliest payment whose running paid total reaches its running due total — a correlated MIN or a join on paid_through >= due_through.
Aggregate to the plan first (BOOL_AND for "all on time", COUNT(*) FILTER (…) per instalment number), then to the cohort.
followups: Cohorts whose last instalments are not yet due are excluded here. How would you report the most recent cohorts honestly, and what does "on time so far" mean?
The team wants a grace period before an instalment counts as late. Where does it go in your query, and how would you show the effect of choosing one grace period over another?
A refund for part of the purchase shrinks the remaining instalments. How would you model it so this report still applies payments correctly?
At tens of millions of plans, how would you compute this incrementally each day rather than recomputing every plan's running totals?

rules.ask: A customer pays an instalment in two halves. Which instalment does your second payment get matched to, and which one should it complete?
How does your comparison treat a payment at 15:00 UTC on the due date, and what type is due_date?
What does your "all on time" test return for a plan whose fourth instalment was never paid?
Payments carry no instalment number. How does your query decide which instalment a payment belongs to when one payment covers more than one?
Would an average of days late tell this team more or less than the share of on-time plans? What would you add next to it?

templates.title: Drawer discrepancy: runs of consecutive cash transactions whose net equals the shortfall
templates.subtopic: subarrays with a given sum over signed values, per-group state, shortest match

sections.scenario: At the end of a shift, a seller counts the cash drawer and compares it with what the point of sale expected. When the drawer is short (or over), the manager reviews the shift's cash transactions — sales, refunds and paid-outs — looking for a stretch of consecutive transactions whose net matches the difference exactly: for example a run that may have been rung up twice, or cash taken for a stretch of sales that never reached the drawer. You are writing the function that finds those candidate runs so the review starts from a short list, not from the whole shift.
sections.problem: Implement discrepancy_runs(txns, shortfalls). txns lists (shift_id, amount_cents, voided) in the order they were rung up: positive amounts are cash taken in, negative amounts cash paid out (refunds, paid-outs). shortfalls maps each shift under review to its discrepancy in cents (expected minus counted; negative for an overage; never 0). A run of a shift is a sequence of consecutive transactions of that shift whose amounts sum exactly to the shift's discrepancy. {{shift_rule}} {{void_rule}} For every shift in shortfalls, return (count, shortest): count is the number of runs, and shortest is (first_pos, last_pos) — the positions in txns of the first and last transaction of the run with the fewest transactions, ties going to the run that starts first — or None when there is no run. Return a dict {shift_id: (count, shortest)}.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 transactions. Amounts are non-zero integers; refunds make some negative, so the net of a run can go down as it grows. Expected: O(n) time. Checking every start for every end is O(n²) and far too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical amounts and shifts. A matching run is only a place to start a review, never evidence of what happened or of who handled the drawer; the output names transactions, not people.
sections.criteria: Prefix sums with a per-shift hash map of counts; the empty prefix seeded; negative amounts and overages handled; the shortest run from the latest matching prefix with the earlier-start tie-break; positions in the original list; shifts kept apart, a shift with no transactions reported and shifts outside shortfalls left out (Hard+); voided transactions skipped and not counted in length (Very Hard); O(n); credible discussion of output size, ranking and running it at warehouse scale.

clarifications.q: Are positions counted within the shift or in the whole list?
clarifications.a: In the whole txns list, 0-based, so the manager can find the transactions.

clarifications.q: Can a run have one transaction?
clarifications.a: Yes, if its amount equals the discrepancy.

clarifications.q: Two runs have the same length.
clarifications.a: The one that starts earlier is the shortest.

clarifications.q: The shift is over by 7.50.
clarifications.a: Its discrepancy is -750: look for runs whose net is -750.

clarifications.q: Can I use two pointers, growing and shrinking a window?
clarifications.a: Only if every amount were positive. Refunds make that approach miss runs.

hints: The net of transactions i+1..j is prefix[j] - prefix[i]. A run ending at j starts after every earlier point where the prefix was prefix[j] - discrepancy.
Keep, per shift, a dict from prefix value to how many times it has occurred — and the latest point it occurred, which gives the shortest run ending at j.
Start each shift's dict with the empty prefix (value 0 before its first transaction).
followups: The manager wants every run, not just the count and the shortest. How large can that output be, and how would you present it so it is still useful?
Runs that are exact matches by coincidence are common in a busy shift with round prices. How would you rank candidate runs so the likeliest explanation comes first?
The point of sale stores transactions for thousands of sellers in a warehouse. How would you run this check for every short drawer each night in SQL or Spark, and what makes it hard to express there?
A discrepancy may also come from two separate mistakes. How would you find pairs of non-overlapping runs whose nets add up to it, and what does that cost?

rules.ask: A refund of -5.00 sits in the middle of a run. What does your window do when the running net goes down as it grows?
How many (start, end) pairs does a 200 000-transaction shift have, and how long would checking them take?
What does your map hold before the shift's first transaction, and which run does that entry let you find?
Do positions in your answer refer to the shift's own list or to txns? How do you map them back?
A voided transaction sits between two that together match. Is that a run, and how long is it?

templates.title: Tip pooling: equal shares among those on the clock, rounded once at the end
templates.subtopic: running per-head totals, event ordering at equal times, rounding once

sections.scenario: A point of sale with team management lets a seller pool tips: instead of each tip going to whoever took the payment, it is shared among the team. A large venue uses this exercise's rule: every tip is split equally among the team members on the clock at the moment the payment was taken, and each member's total is rounded to the cent once, at the end of the pay period, not tip by tip. Tips taken when nobody was on the clock are set aside for the manager to allocate. You are writing the payout calculation.
sections.problem: Implement tip_pool(shifts, tips, adjustments). shifts lists (member_id, clock_in, clock_out) in whole seconds; a member is on the clock at second t if clock_in <= t < clock_out. tips lists (payment_id, paid_at, tip_cents). Each tip is split equally among the members on the clock at paid_at, as an exact fraction of a cent. {{shift_rule}} {{adjust_rule}} A member's payout is their exact total rounded to the nearest cent, half a cent rounding up. Tips with nobody on the clock are unassigned. Return (payouts, unassigned): payouts maps every member that appears in shifts to their payout (0 if none), and unassigned is the total of unassigned tips in cents.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 tips and about 36 000 shifts, with a few hundred members on the clock at busy times. clock_in < clock_out; tips are non-negative. Expected: O((n + m) log(n + m)). Visiting every shift per tip, or every member on the clock per tip, is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical team, shifts and tips. Whether and how tips may be pooled is governed by local law and the seller's own policy; this exercise's equal-split rule is a simplification and says nothing about what any seller should do. Member ids are pseudonymous; the output is each member's own payout.
sections.criteria: Half-open shifts with clock-outs before clock-ins before tips at equal times; exact per-tip shares; rounding once per member with half a cent up; members with no tips present; unassigned tips totalled; a member's shifts summed before rounding (Hard+); the last adjustment replacing the tip at its original payment time (Very Hard); a sweep with a running per-head total in O((n + m) log(n + m)); credible discussion of reconciling cents, weighted pools and late shift edits.

clarifications.q: A tip at the exact second a member clocks out.
clarifications.a: They are not on the clock: clock_out is exclusive. A member clocking in at that second is.

clarifications.q: Three members share a 1.00 tip. What do they get?
clarifications.a: 33⅓ cents each, kept exactly; rounding happens once, on each member's total.

clarifications.q: Do the rounded payouts have to add up to the tips?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; rounding each member once can leave a cent or two over or under. That is a follow-up.

clarifications.q: A member has no tips at all.
clarifications.a: They still appear, with 0.

clarifications.q: Can I use floats?
clarifications.a: Not safely: thousands of thirds and sevenths accumulate error, and the half-cent rule needs exact values. Use integers or fractions.Fraction.

hints: Picture a running total: "how much one person on the clock would have earned since the start". Each tip raises it by tip / heads.
A member's share for a shift is that running total at clock-out minus the total at clock-in — no need to touch the member at each tip.
Sort clock-outs, clock-ins and tips together; at equal times process clock-outs, then clock-ins, then tips.
Keep the running total exact: scale by the least common multiple of the head counts that occur, or use Fraction (slower).
followups: The rounded payouts must add up exactly to the pooled tips. Which rounding rule would you use (for example largest remainder), and how do you explain an odd cent to the team?
The venue wants weighted shares (a role with more points gets a larger share). What changes in the running-total idea?
Shifts are edited after the fact (a forgotten clock-out fixed the next day). How would you recompute only what changed?
A member is on the clock in two locations of the same seller at once by mistake. How should the calculation and the data model prevent or flag it?

rules.ask: Where in your code is a value rounded or stored as a float, and what happens to a 1-cent tip shared by three people, a thousand times?
How many shift checks does your loop make for 200 000 tips and 36 000 shifts?
At a busy time 400 people are on the clock. How much work does each tip cost in your solution, and how would a running per-head total avoid it?
How large do your exact values get, and why is that acceptable here?
Bisect gives you the head count at a tip. How do you then credit each member without visiting all of them?

templates.title: Earliest free slot in a staff member's calendar, booked as you go
templates.subtopic: longest free run, first fit, lazy range assignment

sections.scenario: A salon takes appointments online. Clients pick a service, and the booking page offers the earliest time one staff member can fit it. In this exercise the calendar opens {{weeks}} weeks ahead (this exercise's rule; check current docs for real booking settings). The calendar is kept in whole minutes, and some minutes can never be booked: the hours the location is closed, the staff member's breaks and appointments already in the book. Requests arrive one after another, and each is booked before the next is answered, so two clients are never offered the same minutes.
sections.problem: Implement book_appointments(horizon, busy, requests). The calendar has horizon minutes, numbered from 0, and minute 0 is Monday 00:00 of the first week in the location's local time. busy is a list of (start, end) half-open ranges: minutes start to end - 1 cannot be booked. Process requests in order. A request ("book", length) books the earliest start s such that minutes s to s + length - 1 are all free and s + length <= horizon. Those minutes stop being free, and the result is s. If no such start exists, nothing changes and the result is -1. {{busy_rule}} {{cancel_rule}} Return a list with one result per request, in request order.
sections.constraints: horizon is at most 80 640 (eight weeks). Up to 12 000 requests and 5 000 busy ranges. Every length is a whole number of minutes, at least 1. Each busy range satisfies 0 <= start < end <= horizon. Once the calendar is full, most requests cannot fit. Scanning the minutes for every request is O(horizon) per request and is too slow; something close to O((B + R) · log horizon) for B busy ranges and R requests is expected.
sections.assumptions: Opening hours, breaks, service lengths and request volumes are hypothetical. One staff member, one location, one time zone. A booking needs no buffer before or after it. The earliest start is the only rule: no preference for mornings or for keeping gaps tidy.
sections.criteria: Half-open ranges, unsorted and overlapping busy ranges, and the horizon end all handled; earliest start, not best fit; failed requests leave the calendar unchanged; (Very Hard) cancellations free exactly the booking's minutes once and return -1 for failed or repeated cancels; a structure that answers "nothing fits" quickly and finds the earliest fit in logarithmic time, such as a segment tree of free runs with lazy assignment; a clear complexity argument, including when a gap list is good enough.

clarifications.q: Can a booking start at a minute where a busy range ends?
clarifications.a: Yes. Ranges are half-open, so (60, 120) leaves minute 120 free.

clarifications.q: Are the busy ranges sorted, and can they overlap?
clarifications.a: Neither is promised. They can arrive in any order, overlap and touch.

clarifications.q: Can an appointment run across midnight or across a busy range?
clarifications.a: Across midnight, yes, if every minute is free (it is a single minute line). Never across a busy minute.

clarifications.q: What if a request is longer than the whole calendar?
clarifications.a: Then it cannot fit, and its result is -1.

clarifications.q: Does a request that fails change anything?
clarifications.a: No. The calendar stays as it was.

hints: A request fits only if some free run is at least length long. What would you store per node of a tree over the minutes so that the longest free run inside the node is known?

Store, per node, the longest free run, the free run at its left edge and the free run at its right edge. A parent combines its children with left.suffix + right.prefix for the run that crosses the middle.

To find the earliest start, walk down from the root: go left if the left child holds a long enough run, take the crossing run if it is long enough, and go right otherwise. Booking and freeing are range assignments, so you need lazy propagation.
followups: A sorted list of free gaps also works. When is it faster than the tree, and what calendar makes it slow?
A service needs 10 minutes of clean-up after it, which another booking may not use but which may overlap closing time. What changes?
A client may book with any of several staff members, and the earliest start across all of them wins, ties to the staff member listed first. How do you answer without querying every calendar in turn?
Bookings arrive from several web servers at once. Where does the earliest-fit decision have to be serialised, and what does a client see when two of them race for the same minutes?

rules.ask: Once the calendar is full, every request scans all {{weeks}} weeks of minutes and fails. How many steps is that for 12 000 requests, and how could you answer "nothing fits" in one step?
How many gaps does the list hold in the worst case, and what calendar would make every request walk past most of them?
Why do you need a node's prefix and suffix free runs as well as its longest run? Give two children whose longest runs are both too short while their parent can still fit the request.
Your search runs in C, but what is its complexity per request, and what happens if the calendar is kept in seconds instead of minutes?
A heap gives the longest gap, not the earliest one that fits. How do you get the earliest start that fits from it?

templates.title: Which open invoices does a lump payment cover?
templates.subtopic: exact subset sums, counting matches, ambiguity

sections.scenario: A seller sends invoices to a business customer and has up to {{max_open}} of them open at once. The customer sometimes pays several invoices with one bank transfer and does not say which ones. The seller's bookkeeping assistant wants to mark the right invoices as paid, but only when there is exactly one set of open invoices the transfer can be paying. If several sets fit, a person decides. If none fits, the transfer is a partial payment or a mistake, and that is a different workflow.
sections.problem: Implement match_invoices(invoices, payment). invoices is a list of (invoice_id, amount) open items with unique ids, and payment is the transfer amount, at least 1. All amounts are integer cents. Count the different sets of open items whose amounts add up to exactly payment. Two sets are different when they contain different invoice ids, even if their amounts are the same. Return (count, ids), where ids lists the invoice ids of the only matching set, in the order they appear in invoices, when count == 1, and [] otherwise. {{amount_rule}} {{credit_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to {{max_open}} open items. Amounts are up to $250 000 in cents, so payments reach hundreds of millions of cents and a table indexed by every sum up to the payment does not fit. Trying all 2ⁿ sets is far too slow; something close to O(2^(n/2) · n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Amounts, counts and customers are hypothetical. Every invoice is open for its full amount (no partial payments in this exercise). The transfer pays whole invoices, with no fee taken out and no rounding.
sections.criteria: Counts sets by invoice, not by amount; the empty set never matches; ids only when the count is exactly 1, in input order; (Very Hard) credit notes with negative amounts handled without pruning that assumes positive amounts; a meet-in-the-middle count with a hash map or sorted halves, with the reasoning for why a DP over sums and every-subset search both fail; integer cents throughout; a sensible view of when to match automatically and when to ask a person.

clarifications.q: Does the empty set count?
clarifications.a: No. The payment is at least 1 cent, and the empty set adds up to 0.

clarifications.q: Two invoices have the same amount. Is a set with the first one different from the set with the second?
clarifications.a: Yes. They are different invoices, so the count includes both sets, and the result is ambiguous.

clarifications.q: Why not return a matching set even when there are several?
clarifications.a: Because the seller would mark the wrong invoices paid half the time. Ambiguity goes to a person, so you return the count and no ids.

clarifications.q: Can the count be large?
clarifications.a: Yes, with many similar amounts. Return the exact number.

clarifications.q: In what order are the ids returned?
clarifications.a: In the order the invoices appear in the input list.

hints: Split the invoices into two halves. Every set is a set from the left half plus a set from the right half.
List the 2^(n/2) sums of each half. For every left sum s, how many right sums equal payment - s? A dictionary of counts answers that in O(1).
If the total is exactly 1, remember which left subset gave the match. You can find the matching right subset afterwards, because its sum is unique.
followups: Amounts are small, say under $50 each, and there are 300 invoices. Which approach would you use then, and why?
The customer may have taken an early-payment discount of up to 2% per invoice (this exercise's rule). How would you match with that tolerance, and what happens to ambiguity?
The customer often pays the oldest invoices first. How would you use that to rank several matching sets for the person reviewing them?
Thousands of sellers receive transfers every hour. How would you run this as a service, and which cases would you never try to match automatically?

rules.ask: How many sets are there with {{max_open}} open items, and how long would checking them all take at ten million a second?
How large is your table when one invoice is $250 000, and can it count the matching sets, or only say whether one exists?
Your pruning stops when the sum passes the payment. What happens to that rule {{credit_hint}}, and how many nodes does your search visit when the payment is about half the total?
Give three invoices and a payment where taking the largest invoice that fits first finds no match although one exists.
Your dictionary holds 2^(n/2) sums. How much memory is that for {{max_open}} items, and could a sorted list with two pointers use less?

templates.title: Debug the seller's daily sales summary
templates.subtopic: local dates, offline payments, tips, refunds by day

sections.scenario: A seller with locations in several countries opens the daily sales summary in their dashboard each morning. Support has passed on several complaints about it. A bar on the west coast sees last night's late sales on today's report. A café that ran in offline mode during a network outage sees yesterday's sales on today's report, when the device reconnected. Gross sales do not match the till because they include tips. A sale refunded this week changed a report the seller had already closed last week. A $5 partial refund on a $60 order wiped out the whole $60. The summary code below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix daily_summary(payments, refunds, locations) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. locations maps each location id to its fixed UTC offset in minutes, positive east of UTC (for example −300 for UTC−5 and 600 for UTC+10). A location's local date for a UTC timestamp is the calendar date of that timestamp plus the offset.
  2. payments are dicts {"id", "location", "taken_at", "forwarded_at", "amount", "tip", "status"}. Timestamps are ISO 8601 strings in UTC. amount and tip are integer cents. forwarded_at is None for an online payment. For an offline payment it is when the device forwarded the payment after reconnecting, and status may then be "declined". Only "completed" payments count. A payment belongs to the location's local date of taken_at.
  3. refunds are dicts {"payment", "refunded_at", "amount"} for completed payments, in any order. A payment can have several partial refunds. A refund belongs to the local date of refunded_at, at the payment's location, and subtracts its own amount. Tips are never refunded in this exercise.
  4. Output. A dict keyed "<location>/<YYYY-MM-DD>" for every location and local date with at least one completed payment or refund. Each value is {"payments", "gross", "tips", "refunds", "net"}: the number of completed payments, the sum of their amounts (tips excluded), the sum of their tips, the sum of refunds made that day, and gross - refunds, which can be negative.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. All arithmetic stays in integer cents. Up to 200 000 payments, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Offsets are fixed for this exercise, with no daylight-saving changes. Amounts, locations and timings are hypothetical, and how long a device may stay offline is this exercise's rule (check current docs for real limits). Refunds never exceed what was paid.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its seller-facing symptom; local dates from the location's offset with the right sign; offline payments dated by when they were taken; declined payments excluded; tips reported apart from gross; refunds on their own local date and for their own amount; integer cents throughout; minimal, linear fixes, with a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Which day does an offline payment belong to?
clarifications.a: The day it was taken. Forwarding only tells the processor about it later.

clarifications.q: If a refund on Thursday is for a sale on Monday, does Monday's summary change?
clarifications.a: No. Monday stays as the seller closed it, and Thursday shows the refund. That day can have a negative net.

clarifications.q: Are tips part of gross sales?
clarifications.a: No. They are reported in their own column and belong to the staff, not to sales.

clarifications.q: Which offset applies to a refund?
clarifications.a: The offset of the location where the payment was taken.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Work out the local date of 2026-10-06T02:00:00+00:00 for a location at −300 by hand, then call the helper.
Read every line that touches gross and refunds: which amount does each one add?
Where does the refund loop get its day from?
followups: A location moves from UTC−5 to UTC−4 when daylight saving starts. What would you store instead of a fixed offset, and which days could change?
The summary is precomputed every night. An offline payment taken yesterday is forwarded this morning. Which rows do you recompute, and how does the seller learn that yesterday changed?
A seller asks for "sales by the hour" across all locations in one chart. Whose local time do you use, and what does the chart look like on a day the clocks change?
Gross sales must reconcile to the money deposited to the seller's bank account. List the reasons the two numbers differ on a given day.

rules.ask: A seller in Sydney closes at 22:00 local time. Which UTC date do those sales fall on, and which date does the seller expect?
With named time zones, a local day can have 23 or 25 hours. What does your summary report for those days, and what do you key rows by?
An offline payment is declined when it is finally forwarded. What did the seller's device show at the time, and what does the summary show now?
If refunds restated the sale's day, how would a seller's closed books from last week change, and who would notice?
Where does your code divide money, and what type comes out? Keep the report in integer cents and say where formatting belongs.

templates.title: Item library and inventory across locations and channels
templates.subtopic: catalogue sync, per-location overrides, stock counts, conflicts

sections.scenario: A point-of-sale platform serves about {{sellers}} sellers. Each seller keeps one item library: items, variations (size, colour), prices, modifiers and categories, up to {{max_items}} items for the largest. A seller can have up to {{max_locations}} locations, and a location can override an item's price, hide an item or track its own stock. The same items are sold in person on registers and tablets, and online through the seller's online store. When a seller changes a price, it should reach every register and the online store within {{sync_target}}. When the last unit sells in a shop, the online store should stop selling it soon after.
sections.problem: Design how the item library and stock counts are stored, changed and synced across locations and channels, and how they reach analytics. Cover the data model for items, variations, per-location overrides and stock; how a change made on one device or in the dashboard reaches the others; how stock changes from sales, returns, receiving and manual counts are recorded; what happens when two edits conflict; how the online store avoids selling stock that a shop has just sold; and the tables analysts use for sales by item and stock over time.
sections.constraints: Registers may be offline for hours and must keep selling. Stock can go negative when a shop sells an item the system thought was out of stock, and that must be visible, not hidden. Edits come from the dashboard, from registers, from the online store and from bulk imports of thousands of rows. Analytics must answer "how many units of this variation did location X have at 18:00 last Friday?"
sections.assumptions: All volumes, limits and targets are hypothetical. You may use common building blocks: a relational store, a change stream, a cache, a message queue and a warehouse. Price and stock rules here are this exercise's rules; check current docs for any real product behaviour.
sections.criteria: Item definitions separated from stock; per-variation, per-location stock derived from a change log with reasons; physical counts treated as set-at-a-time events; a versioned change feed per seller for devices; explicit conflict rules with an audit trail the seller can see; offline sales merged without hiding negative stock; a clear answer on overselling between shops and the online store; analytics tables for sales by item and stock at a point in time; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is stock tracked per item or per variation?
clarifications.a: Per variation and per location. An item with three sizes has three stock counts at each location.

clarifications.q: What does a location override look like?
clarifications.a: A price, a visibility flag or a tax setting for one variation at one location. Anything not overridden comes from the library.

clarifications.q: What happens when a register sells offline?
clarifications.a: It records the sale and a stock decrement locally and uploads both when it reconnects, possibly hours later.

clarifications.q: Who wins when two people edit the same price at once?
clarifications.a: You decide and explain it. The seller must be able to see what happened.

clarifications.q: Does the online store have its own stock?
clarifications.a: In this exercise it sells from one location's stock, chosen by the seller.

hints: Separate the item definition (rarely changes, read everywhere) from stock (changes on every sale). They have different write rates and different conflict rules.
Store stock as a log of changes with reasons (sale, return, receive, count, adjustment) and derive on-hand counts from it. A physical count sets the value at a moment; it is not a delta.
Give every library change a version per seller, and let each device ask for "everything since version N".
followups: A register comes back online after four hours with 300 sales. Walk through what happens to stock, the online store and the dashboard.
A stock count at 09:00 says 12 units, but a sale recorded offline at 08:55 arrives at 11:00. What is on hand now, and why?
A bulk import changes 40 000 prices at once. How do registers receive it without stalling, and what happens to a sale rung up halfway through?
Analysts want "stock at 18:00 on any day" for every variation and location. Do you store snapshots, replay the change log, or both, and what does each cost at {{max_items}} items?

rules.ask: Two devices with clocks 90 seconds apart edit the same price. Which edit wins under your rule, and what does the seller see?
A counter merges sales from many devices, but a physical count sets the value to 12. How does your structure represent a "set" that must override earlier deltas but not later ones?
An offline sale from yesterday afternoon arrives this morning. Which snapshots are now wrong, and how do you fix them?
Who holds stock for an online order that has not been picked yet, and what happens if a shop sells that unit in the meantime?
A price changes and one register still shows the old one from cache. How long can that last, and what price does the sale record?

incidents: A seller with {{max_locations}} locations bulk-imports a new price list at 08:55. Registers opening at 09:00 show a mix of old and new prices for twenty minutes.
A shop's register is offline all afternoon on a busy day. When it reconnects, the online store has sold eight units that the shop had already sold, and that location's on-hand count goes to −8.

templates.title: Peer-to-peer payment events into analytics, with the right final state
templates.subtopic: state machines, out-of-order and duplicate events, late reversals

sections.scenario: A peer-to-peer payments app lets people send money to each other. About {{daily_payments}} payments are made a day. Events about each payment come from {{client_kinds}} kinds of producers, such as the phone apps, the web app and the service that moves the money. In this exercise's model a payment is sent, may be pending (for example while the recipient has not accepted it), and then becomes completed or cancelled. A completed payment can still be reversed up to {{reversal_window}} later (this exercise's rule). Product and finance teams want dashboards, refreshed every {{freshness}}, of payment counts and amounts by state, day and region, and they need the totals to match what actually happened. Individual people's payments never appear in analytics outputs; only aggregates do.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that turns these events into analytics tables. Cover the event contract (what every producer must send), how duplicates and out-of-order events are handled, how the current state of each payment is derived, how late reversals and corrections change totals that were already published, what the published tables look like at their grain, how the pipeline is backfilled and rerun, and how you show that the published totals are right.
sections.constraints: Events from phones can arrive hours late, after the phone reconnects. The same event can arrive more than once. A completed event can arrive before its pending event. Totals for a day can change after the day ends, and finance must know when and why. Amounts are integer minor units in the payment's currency. No table that analysts query may expose one person's payments.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, windows and freshness targets are hypothetical. The service that moves the money is the authority on whether a payment completed, and it emits an event for every change it makes. Phone and web events describe what the person saw and did. You may use common building blocks: a partitioned log, a stream processor, object storage, a warehouse.
sections.criteria: A clear event contract with event ids, payment ids and the authoritative source; a state machine whose result does not depend on arrival order, with invalid transitions flagged; deduplication with a stated memory window; late reversals applied to the right day with "first published" versus "current" totals; tables at a stated grain with privacy-preserving aggregates; deterministic reruns and backfills; reconciliation against the money-movement service as proof of correctness; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Which source decides the final state?
clarifications.a: The money-movement service. Client events add context, such as where in the app the payment started, and never override it.

clarifications.q: Can a payment go from cancelled to completed?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise's model. If events say so, that is a data problem to flag, not a state to show.

clarifications.q: Which day does a payment belong to?
clarifications.a: You choose and explain it: the day it was sent, the day it completed, or both, for different questions. A reversal belongs to its own day for some reports.

clarifications.q: Do dashboards show individual payments?
clarifications.a: No. Only aggregates, with small groups suppressed or combined.

clarifications.q: How late can an event be?
clarifications.a: Client events up to two days; a reversal up to {{reversal_window}} after completion.

hints: Give every event a stable event id and every payment a payment id, and decide which fields are the payment's state and which are context.
Define the allowed transitions and a rank for each state, so that applying events in any order ends in the same state. Keep the event history so that you can explain the state.
Keep "as of now" totals separate from "as first published" totals, so that changes to past days are visible as changes.
followups: A completed event arrives before sent and pending. Walk through what your state table holds after each event.
A reversal arrives {{reversal_window}} after a payment completed, at the very end of the window. Which published numbers change, and how does a finance analyst see the change?
One phone app version sends every event twice with different event ids. How do you notice, and how do you fix the totals?
Leadership wants "payments completed in under a minute" as a metric. Which events and timestamps do you trust for it, and why not the phone's clock?
At {{daily_payments}} payments a day, recomputing every payment's state from history each run is too slow. What do you keep incrementally, and how do you rerun one day from scratch?

rules.ask: Events from the phone and from the money-movement service disagree, and the phone's clock is ahead. Which state does your rule pick, and is it right?
How long do you remember event ids, and what happens to a duplicate that arrives after that window?
A reversal arrives {{reversal_window}} after the payment. Your stream window closed long ago. Where does that change land?
Which tables contain a person's identifier, who can query them, and how do the published tables avoid showing one person's activity?
Exactly-once delivery inside the pipeline does not stop a producer from sending the same fact twice. What does?

incidents: A phone app release sends cancelled instead of completed for one screen's payments; client events and money-movement events disagree for 3% of payments for six hours.
A batch of reversals is processed late, with reversal times up to {{reversal_window}} in the past, and the published completed amount for the days they touch drops by 0.4% overnight.

templates.title: Seller accounts as data — businesses, locations, devices, team members, permissions and what each location sold on a date
templates.subtopic: effective-dated hierarchy, device pairing, permission history, location business dates

permission_model: four fixed roles (owner, admin, manager, staff)
fixed roles plus custom permission sets the owner can edit

sections.scenario: A point-of-sale platform serves {{sellers}} sellers, from a single market stall to chains of up to {{max_locations}} locations. A business has locations (each with an address, a time zone and opening and closing dates); devices (card readers, registers and phones running the point-of-sale app) paired to one location at a time; and team members who are assigned to some locations and hold a role. In this exercise's model permissions come from {{permission_model}}: for example, who may issue refunds, open the cash drawer, see reports or edit items. Things change constantly: about {{device_moves}} of devices are re-paired to another location each month, locations open, close and reopen, team members leave and come back, and roles are edited. Sellers want daily sales per location in each location's own business date; an owner checking a disputed refund wants to know who was allowed to issue refunds at that location on that day.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: the entities (business, location, device, team member, role or permission set, and the assignments between them) with keys; how history is kept for device pairings, location attributes, team assignments and permission definitions, so the state on any past date can be reconstructed; how a payment or order gets its location and business date, and why that is fixed when the payment happens; the daily sales fact per location and the dimensions it joins to (as-of-date versus current attributes); and the query shape for "who could issue refunds at location L on date D". Say what personal data about team members reaches the warehouse.
sections.constraints: A sale's location never changes after the fact, even when its device moves later. Daily sales use the location's business date in its own time zone. Any past date's permissions for any team member at any location are reconstructable. Ids are stable; names change. Money is integer cents. Team members appear in analytics by id and role only; contact details stay in the operational system.
sections.assumptions: Seller counts, location counts and move rates are hypothetical. A business operates in one currency in this exercise. A device belongs to exactly one location at a time and to one business forever. A team member can work at several locations of the same business.
sections.criteria: Entities with stable ids and effective-dated relationships (pairings, assignments, roles, permission-set versions, location attributes); location, time zone and business date stamped on the payment at write time; a daily sales fact by location and business date with as-of and current dimension options; a correct "who could refund on date D" walk; non-overlapping intervals with a stated boundary convention; team-member data minimised; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a device be paired to two locations at once?
clarifications.a: No. One location at a time; a move ends one pairing and starts the next.

clarifications.q: Does a payment carry its location?
clarifications.a: The device sends its device id and the location it believes it is in. Decide which you trust and when it is stamped.

clarifications.q: Can a location change time zone?
clarifications.a: Rarely, when it moves. The business date of a sale uses the time zone in force when the sale happened.

clarifications.q: Is a role per business or per location?
clarifications.a: The role is per team member and business; assignments say which locations they work at. Permissions apply only at assigned locations.

clarifications.q: Can an owner edit a permission set?
clarifications.a: Yes, with custom sets. An edit applies to everyone holding the set from that moment and never changes the past.

hints: Model every relationship that changes as its own effective-dated table with valid_from and valid_to, not as a column on the entity.
Stamp location_id, the location's time zone and the business date on each payment when it is written; deriving them later from the device's current pairing rewrites history.
Permission sets need versions: a role points at a set, and the set's version in force on a date says what it allowed.
followups: A reader moved from the café to the kiosk on Tuesday at 14:00. Show the rows for its pairing and how Monday's and Tuesday's sales are attributed.
Write the query shape for "who could issue refunds at location L on date D", walking assignments, roles and permission-set versions.
A seller with {{max_locations}} locations reorganises them into regions. Do last year's reports group by the regions then or now, and how does your model offer both?
A location closes and reopens six months later at a new address in another time zone. Is it the same location, and what happens to its reports?
At {{sellers}} sellers, how much history do these effective-dated tables hold, and how do you serve a seller dashboard that asks for the state on a date in milliseconds?

rules.ask: The reader moved to another location yesterday. With the location on the device row, which location do last week's sales show?
A location in Honolulu closes its till at 22:00 local. On which business date do its last sales land in your fact, and why?
The owner removed refund rights from managers last month. Can your model say who could refund at the downtown location in the week before that?
How do you stop two pairings for the same device overlapping, and is valid_to inclusive or exclusive?
A team member left in March. Their refunds from February still need a name in the audit. What do you keep, and what do you never copy into the warehouse?

incidents: A bulk re-pairing tool, run by mistake for a seller with {{max_locations}} locations, moved every reader to the flagship for an hour. Payments in that hour were stamped with the flagship, and the other locations' daily sales dropped.
An owner edited a custom permission set to remove refund rights; the warehouse held only the current definition, so an audit of who could refund last quarter came back with today's permissions.
New locations were created without a time zone and defaulted to UTC. For weeks their business dates were shifted, and daily sales did not match the till reports sellers printed.

templates.title: Instalment plans as data — purchases, schedules, payments, late fees, rescheduling and refunds that shrink what is left
templates.subtopic: versioned schedules, payment allocation, fees as charges, refund allocation, receivables on a date

schedule_rule: four instalments, the first at checkout and the rest every two weeks
four instalments, the first at checkout and the rest every two weeks, or six monthly instalments for larger orders
late_fee_rule: a fixed late fee when an instalment is still unpaid 10 days after its due date, with all fees on a purchase capped at 25% of the order
a late fee charged once per missed instalment after a 3-day grace period, capped per purchase

sections.scenario: A buy-now-pay-later service lets a shopper split a purchase at a merchant into instalments. In this exercise's rule (check current docs) a plan is {{schedule_rule}}; the instalments are equal except that any leftover cents go on the first. The shopper's card is charged automatically on each due date; a failed charge is retried, and the shopper can pay early or move a due date within limits. In this exercise {{late_fee_rule}}. Merchants can refund all or part of a purchase at any time; about {{partial_refund_share}} of plans see a partial refund, which in this exercise reduces the remaining instalments starting from the last one, and refunds the shopper's money only for any amount beyond what is still unpaid. About {{monthly_plans}} plans start each month. Finance wants receivables outstanding on any date; the product team wants the share of instalments paid on time by purchase cohort; support wants to explain any plan's history to its shopper.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: purchases and plans; schedules as versions (original, after a reschedule, after a refund), each with instalments carrying due date and amount; payment attempts (succeeded, failed, retried) and how a successful payment is allocated to instalments (including early and partial payments); late fees as their own charges, with waivers; refunds and how each is allocated to instalments and, beyond that, to money returned; plan status. State the invariants that must hold on every plan, and the facts behind "receivables outstanding on a date", "on-time rate by purchase-month cohort and instalment number" and "late fees charged and waived per month".
sections.constraints: Money is integer cents. For every plan at every moment: Σ current instalment amounts = order amount − refunds allocated to instalments, and Σ payments allocated = Σ instalments paid. An instalment's due date at the time a fee was charged must be reconstructable. Fees never exceed the cap in this exercise's rule. Analytics never draw conclusions about a person's credit-worthiness or eligibility; they measure plans and instalments.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, schedules, fee rules and shares are hypothetical and are this exercise's rules, not a statement of any real product's terms. One currency per plan. Each shopper's local date decides due dates in this exercise.
sections.criteria: Plans with versioned schedules and instalments; payment attempts separated from allocations; leftover-cent rule explicit; fees and waivers as their own records with the cap enforced; refund allocation from the last instalment with any excess returned; invariants as checkable sums; receivables and on-time rates read from versions in force on a date; no person-level credit judgements; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: How is $100.01 split into four?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, 2501 + 2500 + 2500 + 2500 cents: leftover cents go on the first instalment.

clarifications.q: Does a reschedule create a new plan?
clarifications.a: No. The plan keeps its id; a new schedule version replaces the remaining instalments' due dates. The old version stays readable.

clarifications.q: A merchant refunds $30 on a plan with $50 unpaid in two instalments of $25. What happens?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the last instalment drops to 0 and the one before it to $20; nothing is returned to the shopper because the refund is less than what is unpaid.

clarifications.q: Can a late fee be waived?
clarifications.a: Yes, by support, with a reason. The waiver is its own record; the fee row is never deleted.

clarifications.q: What counts as "on time"?
clarifications.a: Paid in full by the end of the due date in the shopper's time zone, against the due date in force when the instalment fell due. You decide how rescheduled instalments are reported.

hints: Keep plans, schedule versions, instalments, payment attempts, payment allocations, fees, waivers and refund allocations as separate tables; a plan's state is derived from them.
Allocation rows (payment → instalment, refund → instalment or money returned) make the invariants checkable with sums.
Receivables on a date are instalment amounts in force on that date minus allocations made by that date, read from versioned rows, never from the plan's current status.
followups: Walk one plan: a $100.01 purchase, the second instalment's charge fails twice and succeeds four days late, then a $30 partial refund. Show the rows each event writes.
A shopper moved the third due date by a week. Is that instalment on time or late in the cohort report, and what does your model let you show either way?
A refund arrives after the plan is fully paid. Where does the money go, and which rows record it?
Finance asks for receivables outstanding at month end, restated when a later refund applies to an earlier purchase. Which date does the refund use, and how is the restatement labelled?
At {{monthly_plans}} new plans a month with a schedule version on every change, how do you partition and serve "the plan as it stood on a date" for support?

rules.ask: The second instalment's due date moved and then a partial refund changed its amount. With one row updated in place, what was due on the original date, and was the late fee right?
Show the cents for an order of 10001. Where do the leftover cents go, and how does a refund that shrinks the last instalment keep the sum exact?
Which of these measures is about plans and which would be a judgement about a person? What does this model refuse to store or show?
The fee was charged and later waived, then the instalment was paid. How does the fee report for that month look before and after the waiver?
A shopper in a zone behind UTC pays at 21:00 local on the due date. Is it on time in your model, and which date column decides?

incidents: A release overwrote due dates in place when shoppers rescheduled. Late fees charged under this exercise's rule ({{late_fee_rule}}) can no longer be shown to have been correct, and support cannot tell shoppers what was due when.

Partial refunds (about {{partial_refund_share}} of plans) were applied to the next instalment instead of the last; the next charge dropped to 0, later instalments were unchanged, and on-time rates rose for the wrong reason.
A refund on fully paid plans was recorded as reducing remaining instalments, of which there were none; the amount was dropped and shoppers were not refunded.

templates.title: Point-of-sale orders as data — line items, modifiers, discounts, taxes, tips, split tenders and partial refunds
templates.subtopic: order line grain, allocation with exact rounding, tax lines, tenders and refund allocation

tax_rule: a sales tax is added on top of prices, and some items are exempt
prices already include tax, at two rates depending on the item
tip_rule: entered on the reader before payment, or, at table-service sellers, added to a signed receipt and adjusted after the order closes
added to a signed receipt and adjusted after the order closes, up to a day later

sections.scenario: Sellers ring up about {{daily_orders}} orders a day. An order has line items (an item variation, a quantity and a unit price), each with optional priced modifiers (an extra shot, a larger size); discounts can apply to one line or to the whole order, as a percentage or a fixed amount. In this exercise, {{tax_rule}}. Tips are {{tip_rule}}. About {{split_share}} of orders are paid with more than one tender: two cards, card and cash, or a gift card and a card. Later, a seller can refund part of an order: some units of one line, or an amount with no item. The seller's reports must show net sales per item and modifier, discounts given, tax collected per tax, tips per team member and tender mix, and every report must agree with the money that actually moved.
sections.problem: Design the data model for orders and their payments. Cover: order, line, modifier, discount (with its application to lines), tax (per line and tax), service charges, tenders (type, amount, tip, card details kept to what reporting needs), refunds (per line and quantity, or amount only) and their allocation to tenders; how an order-level discount and the tax on it are allocated to lines so that every line and the order total agree to the cent; and the facts at their grains: order line, tender, refund line. Define net sales, and the invariants that tie lines, taxes, tenders and refunds together.
sections.constraints: Money is integer cents. Σ line totals (after discounts and tax) + service charges = order total; Σ tenders = order total + tips. A refund never returns more than a line's paid amount for its quantity, or more than a tender received. Allocations are computed once, stored, and never recomputed with different rounding. Card details beyond brand, entry method and last four digits never reach analytics.
sections.assumptions: Order volumes, tax rules and shares are hypothetical; tax rules here are this exercise's rules and not tax advice. One currency per order. Items and modifiers reference an item library that changes over time; the order keeps the name and price at the time of sale.
sections.criteria: Order, line, modifier, discount application, tax line, tender and refund entities at clear grains; exact allocation with stored shares; invariants for lines, totals, tenders and refunds; refunds as new rows referencing lines and tenders with per-tender caps; tips apart from sales; point-in-time item names and prices on lines; card data minimised; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: How is a 10% order discount split across lines?
clarifications.a: Pro rata by line amount, rounded so the line shares add up exactly to the discount (for example, largest remainder). Store the result.

clarifications.q: Is a tip part of net sales?
clarifications.a: No. Tips belong to the team, are reported separately, and are not taxed in this exercise.

clarifications.q: A gift card and a card paid an order; one item is refunded. Which tender gets the money back?
clarifications.a: Your rule, stated. A common choice refunds to the original tenders in a fixed order, never more than each paid.

clarifications.q: Does a refund return the tax?
clarifications.a: Yes, the tax on the refunded part, allocated the same way as when sold.

clarifications.q: Can a line's price change after the sale?
clarifications.a: No. A correction is a refund and a new sale.

hints: The order line is the grain for sales; the tender is the grain for money received. Keep both and tie them with invariants.
Allocate order-level amounts once with an exact method (largest remainder or "last line takes the rest") and store the per-line shares.
Refunds are their own lines referencing the original line and quantity, plus refund-tender rows; never edit the sale.
followups: Work an order: two coffees at 450 with a 60-cent modifier on one, a pastry at 375, a 10% order discount and the tax rule given. Show every line's discount, tax and total in cents and prove the invariants.
Half of the coffees are refunded on an order split between a gift card and a card. Which rows are written, and how does net sales per item change?
A tip is adjusted after the order closes. Which fact changes, on which business date, and how does the tender mix stay right?
The item is renamed and repriced next month. How do this month's reports still show what was sold?
At {{daily_orders}} orders a day, which facts do you keep at line grain for years, and how do you rebuild daily summaries when a refund lands weeks later?

rules.ask: Three lines each get a third of a 100-cent discount. What do your rounded shares add up to, and how do you make them equal the discount exactly?
Net sales by item needs the discount and tax per line. Where do those live if the order is one row?
An item paid partly by gift card and partly by card is refunded. How much goes back to each, and what stops a tender from being refunded more than it paid?
A tip is adjusted after close and the tender row is re-sent. How do you avoid counting the payment twice in the tender mix?
Which card details does reporting actually need, and what keeps the rest out of the warehouse?

incidents: Order-level discounts were allocated to lines with each share rounded on its own. In about 0.4% of orders lines summed to one cent more or less than the order total, and net sales per item no longer reconciled with tenders.

With {{split_share}} of orders on several tenders, partial refunds were all sent back to the first tender. Some gift cards received more than they had paid, and some card tenders show refunds above their charge.
Tips are {{tip_rule}}. After a release, each tip adjustment arrived as a new tender row; payments counted per order doubled for those orders, and tender mix shifted toward cards.

templates.title: Gift cards and store credit as data — issuance, loads, redemptions across locations, expiry and balances on a date
templates.subtopic: stored-value activity log, concurrent redemption, offline devices, expiry rules, balances on a date

credit_expiry: store credit expires 12 months after it is issued
store credit expires 6 months after its last use

sections.scenario: Sellers sell gift cards, physical (printed in batches, activated at the till) and digital (bought online and emailed). A card is loaded with an amount, can be reloaded, and is redeemed at any of the seller's up to {{max_locations}} locations, often for part of an order with the rest on another tender. A refunded purchase that was paid by gift card goes back onto the card. Sellers also issue store credit for returns; in this exercise gift cards do not expire, but {{credit_expiry}} (this exercise's rule; check current docs and local law, which differ by place). Some readers take payments in offline mode, and in this exercise an offline device may redeem up to {{offline_cap}} from a card whose balance it last saw. There are about {{active_cards}} cards with a balance. Sellers want each card's history, the outstanding balance on any date, and redemptions by location; the issuing location and the redeeming location are often different.
sections.problem: Design the data model for gift cards and store credit. Cover: the instruments (gift card, store credit) and their lifecycle (created, activated, loaded, redeemed, refunded onto, expired, cleared, blocked); an append-only activity record with types, signed effects and keys to the order and location; how a card's balance is read quickly while the activity record stays the truth; how two simultaneous redemptions on the same card are prevented from overdrawing it online, and what happens when offline redemptions arrive later; how expiry is applied and recorded; and the facts behind "outstanding balance per seller on a date", "redemptions by location versus issuing location" and "store credit expiring next month".
sections.constraints: Money is integer cents. A card's balance at any past instant equals the signed sum of its activities up to that instant. An online redemption never takes a balance below zero; an offline one may, and must then be visible and resolved. Expiry is an activity, not a deletion. Card numbers are never stored in analytics; a surrogate card id is.
sections.assumptions: Card counts, caps and expiry rules are hypothetical and are this exercise's rules. One currency per seller. Cards are redeemable only at the issuing seller's locations. The accounting treatment of unredeemed balances is the seller's decision; the model reports amounts and leaves conclusions to them.
sections.criteria: Instruments with a lifecycle; an append-only typed activity record with order, location and device keys; a stored balance kept in step and reconciled nightly; a race-free online redemption; offline activities with occurred and synced times and visible negative balances; expiry as an activity under a versioned rule in local time; balances on a date from occurred time; card numbers kept out of analytics; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is the balance stored on the card or computed?
clarifications.a: Both, if you like: a stored balance for speed, but the activity record is the truth and the two must reconcile.

clarifications.q: Two tills redeem the same card in the same second. What should happen?
clarifications.a: Online, exactly one of them succeeds if the balance covers only one. Say how.

clarifications.q: An offline redemption arrives after the card was emptied online. What then?
clarifications.a: The redemption already happened at the till. Record it, show the negative balance, and route it to the seller; nothing here decides who is at fault.

clarifications.q: Does a balance check count as use?
clarifications.a: No. In this exercise only loads, redemptions and refunds onto the card count as use.

clarifications.q: When does store credit expire under a "since last use" rule?
clarifications.a: The expiry moves each time the credit is used; record the rule version and the computed expiry date.

hints: One append-only activity table per instrument (type, signed amount, order, location, device, occurred_at, synced_at) plus a balance row kept in step in the same transaction for online writes.
Prevent online overdraw with a conditional update on the balance row (balance ≥ amount) or a version check; the activity and the balance change commit together.
Offline activities carry the device's occurred time and a later sync time; balances on a date use occurred time, and late arrivals restate the past.
followups: Walk a card: activated at 5000 at one location, redeemed 3200 at another, a 1200 refund back onto it, then two tills try to redeem 2500 at the same moment. Show the rows and the balance after each.

An offline reader redeems up to {{offline_cap}} from a card that was emptied online in the meantime. What does the seller see, and how does the outstanding balance report for that day change when the offline activity syncs?
Write the definition of "outstanding balance per seller on a date" and say how a late offline activity changes a report already sent.
Under the rule that {{credit_expiry}}, how do you produce "store credit expiring next month" and the expiry activities themselves, and in which time zone?
At {{active_cards}} cards with a balance, how do you serve a balance lookup at the till in milliseconds and still prove nightly that every stored balance equals its activity sum?

rules.ask: A seller asks for the card's balance on 1 March last year. With only the current balance stored, what can you answer?
Show the exact statement that makes two simultaneous 2500 redemptions on a 3000 balance end with one success. What does the loser see?
The offline redemption already happened. Do you reject it on sync, accept it into a negative balance, or something else, and who is told?
The expiry job ran in UTC and some locations are hours behind. Which credits expired a day early, and how do you reverse them without deleting rows?
Which id does the warehouse use for a card, and how does support still find a card from the number on its back?

incidents: After an outage, readers in offline mode synced several hundred redemptions at once; cards redeemed up to {{offline_cap}} offline were also emptied online, and some balances went below zero with no alert to sellers.
The expiry job for store credit ({{credit_expiry}}) ran on UTC dates and expired credit a day early for locations behind UTC; shoppers were turned away at the till with credit they still held.
A data migration replayed a day of load activities. Outstanding balances for a seller with {{max_locations}} locations jumped, and stored balances no longer matched the activity sums.

templates.title: Gift card balances on a date, and cards untouched for twelve months, per seller
templates.subtopic: signed activity sums, end-of-day boundaries, dormancy cutoffs, local dates

sections.scenario: Sellers on a point-of-sale platform sell gift cards. Each card belongs to one seller and is redeemable at any of that seller's locations.
