Every change to a card is a row in gift_card_activities with a kind and a non-negative amount_cents; the kind decides the sign. A printed card exists in gift_cards before it is activated; a card's first activity is always activate. In this exercise gift cards do not expire. Sellers want their outstanding gift card balance on a chosen date, and how much of it sits on cards nobody has used for a year.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns seller_id, cards_with_balance, outstanding_cents, dormant_cards, dormant_cents as of the end of {{as_of_date}}: one row per seller that has at least one card activated by then, ordered by seller_id. A card's balance is the sum of its activities up to the end of the as-of date, signed by kind: {{kinds_rule}} cards_with_balance counts the seller's cards whose balance is above 0, and outstanding_cents sums those balances. A card is dormant when its balance is above 0 and its last activity up to the end of the as-of date fell on or before {{cutoff_date}}, twelve months earlier. dormant_cards and dormant_cents count and sum the dormant cards' balances. {{tz_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). "The end of the as-of date" includes 23:59:59 on that date and excludes 00:00:00 on the next. Activities after the as-of date are ignored for both the balance and the last activity. A seller whose activated cards all have zero balance still gets a row of zeros. The sample has {{cards}} cards and {{activities}} activities; production has hundreds of millions of cards.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, sellers and amounts. Amounts are integer cents. A redemption never exceeds the card's balance at the time, so balances are never negative in this data. Time zones here observe no daylight saving time, but your query should not depend on that.
sections.criteria: Activities signed by kind and summed per card up to the end of the as-of date; last activity limited to the same window and excluding balance checks where stated; the cutoff inclusive of its date and exclusive of the next day's midnight; dormant only with a positive balance; sellers with only spent cards kept; local-date boundaries per seller at the hardest level; deterministic ordering; can explain snapshots for speed and restatement for late data.

clarifications.q: Does a card created but never activated count?
clarifications.a: No. A card counts from its activate activity; until then it holds nothing.

clarifications.q: Is a card whose last activity was exactly on the cutoff date dormant?
clarifications.a: Yes. Last activity on or before the cutoff date means untouched for twelve months.

clarifications.q: A card was untouched for a year on the as-of date but reloaded a week later. Dormant?
clarifications.a: Yes, as of the as-of date. Later activities do not exist yet on that date.

clarifications.q: Does created_at on gift_cards matter?
clarifications.a: No. It is when the card was printed or issued, not when it was activated or used.

clarifications.q: Do I need the location?
clarifications.a: No. Balances are per card and seller, whichever location the activity happened at.

hints: Work out each seller's two boundaries first: the instant the as-of date ends and the instant the day after the cutoff date starts, both at local midnight.
Aggregate activities per card up to the as-of boundary: a signed balance with CASE, and the last activity time with MAX(...) FILTER (WHERE ...).
Then aggregate cards per seller with COUNT(*) FILTER and SUM(...) FILTER, wrapping sums in COALESCE(..., 0).
followups: At hundreds of millions of cards, how would you serve this per seller for any date without summing every activity since the card was activated?
Offline redemptions sync days late with their original occurred_at. How does that change a report already sent for the as-of date, and how would you label it?
Sellers ask for the dormant balance by the location that sold the card. What changes in the query, and where does "the location that sold it" come from?
A rule change makes balance checks count as use. Which part of your query changes, and what happens to last month's numbers?

rules.ask: A printed card was created a year ago and activated yesterday. What does created_at tell you about its dormancy?
Your cutoff is a timestamp twelve months before the end of the as-of date. Is a card whose last activity was at exactly that instant dormant, and is that what the rule says?
A seller's activated cards are all spent. Does that seller still get a row in your result?
Does your last activity include balance checks, and activities after the as-of date?
Which midnight is the end of the as-of date for a seller in Tokyo, and which instant is that in UTC?

incidents: The report for {{as_of_date}} was run with occurred_at::date <= '{{as_of_date}}' in UTC; sellers in zones ahead of UTC saw next-morning redemptions inside the month and the balances they printed at the till disagreed.

A version of the report took the last activity over all time; a seller's year-end dormant balance fell sharply after a reload promotion in the new year, and the earlier report could not be reproduced.

templates.title: Restaurant order flow — tickets to kitchen displays, course timing and table turns in local time
templates.subtopic: local routing, ticket state machines, time-zone-correct metrics

sections.scenario: A point-of-sale product for restaurants runs in about {{locations}} locations across {{time_zones}} time zones. Servers enter orders on handhelds and registers at the front of house; each order becomes a ticket whose items are routed to kitchen display screens at up to {{stations}} stations per location (grill, fry, cold, pastry, bar). Items are grouped into courses: the first course is sent to the kitchen at once, later courses are held and "fired" when the server or the expo station says so. A cook bumps an item or a ticket off the screen when it is done; a bump made by mistake can be recalled. Tables are seated, ordered, paid and cleared. Owners want reports on ticket times per station, the gap between courses, and table turns per location and daypart. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), a location's business day ends at {{close_hour}} local time, so a ticket at 1 a.m. belongs to the previous day's dinner service.
sections.problem: Design the system end to end: how a ticket travels from the front of house to the right kitchen screens quickly and reliably, the event model for tickets, items, courses, bumps and tables, and the analytics. Define precisely: ticket time per station, course gap, and table turn time, including what happens when an item is added, voided or remade after the ticket was sent, when a check is split, and when a party moves tables. Say how every report is placed in the location's own business day and daypart.
sections.constraints: A ticket must appear on the kitchen screen within one second of being sent at p99, including during a busy dinner service. If the location's internet connection drops, the front of house and the kitchen must keep working with each other. Owners with several locations compare them side by side, each in its own local time. Reports for yesterday must be final by 9 a.m. local time; today's numbers may be minutes behind. Device clocks within one location can disagree by a few seconds, sometimes by minutes.
sections.assumptions: All counts, timings and volumes are hypothetical. Each location has a registered address and IANA time zone. Devices in a location share a local network. Menu items carry a station routing set by the owner, and owners rename and re-route stations whenever they like.
sections.criteria: Separates the in-location latency path (local routing over the location's network, a local coordinator or peer delivery with acknowledgements, store-and-forward to the cloud) from the analytics path; stable ids created at order entry and event-sourced state machines for tickets, items, courses and tables that tolerate duplicates and late events; precise metric definitions (kitchen time from fire to bump, guest wait from send, course gap, table turn) with explicit handling of voids, remakes, split checks, moved tables and recalls; UTC instants plus the location's time zone, business day and daypart derived from local time with the {{close_hour}} cut-off and daylight-saving changes; clock-skew handling (server receipt time, per-device offset estimates); station history kept so renames and re-routes do not break trends; percentiles rather than means; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is ticket time measured from when the server sent it, or from when the kitchen screen showed it?
clarifications.a: Owners want both: the time the kitchen spent and the time the guest waited. Define both and say which timestamps each uses.

clarifications.q: Does a held course count toward ticket time while it waits to be fired?
clarifications.a: No. Kitchen time for a course starts when it is fired; the guest's wait between courses is the course gap.

clarifications.q: How should a remake count?
clarifications.a: It is a new item on the same ticket and station, linked to the item it replaces; owners want remakes counted separately, not hidden inside the average.

clarifications.q: What about locations that never close, or that close after the business-day cut-off?
clarifications.a: The {{close_hour}} rule applies to every location in this exercise; a ticket is assigned to the business day in which it was sent.

clarifications.q: Can owners change a location's time zone?
clarifications.a: Only when it was set wrong. Decide whether history moves with the correction.

hints: Separate the latency-critical path inside the location (front of house to kitchen screens) from the path to the cloud for analytics; they need different guarantees.
Give every ticket, item and course a stable id created where the order is entered, and model each as a state machine driven by events, so late and repeated events are harmless.
Store instants in UTC with the location's time zone, and derive the business day and daypart from local time at query or build time, not at the device.
followups: Walk through one table of four with two courses and a remade main: which events are produced, in what order, and what each metric reports for it.
How do the kitchen screens keep receiving tickets when the location's internet is down, and what reaches the cloud when it comes back?
Two devices in the same location disagree on the time by three minutes. Which timestamps do your metrics trust, and how do you detect the skew?
The clocks change for daylight saving in one time zone on a Sunday. Walk through Saturday's late service and Sunday's brunch in your reports.
An owner renames the "grill" station to "hot line" and moves half its items to a new station mid-month. How do ticket-time trends per station stay readable?

rules.ask: The location's internet drops in the middle of dinner service. Which path does a new ticket take to the grill screen now, and what happens to tickets already in flight?
One kitchen screen's clock is four minutes fast. What do your ticket times look like for that station, and how would you find out?
A ticket is sent at 1:30 a.m. local time on the night the clocks go back. Which business day and daypart is it in, and how many minutes long was that night?
One ticket was left on the screen overnight and bumped the next morning. What does it do to your average, and what would you report instead?
A cook bumps a ticket by mistake and recalls it 40 seconds later. What does the event history look like, and what does ticket time report?

incidents: After the clocks go back in one of the {{time_zones}} time zones, Sunday's brunch report for every location in that zone shows a median ticket time of −58 minutes at one station and a table turn of 25 hours.

A busy location's internet connection drops for 40 minutes during dinner service. The kitchen keeps cooking, and when the connection returns about 1,500 events arrive at once, with one kitchen screen's timestamps three minutes ahead of the registers'.

An owner of 120 locations re-routes desserts from the cold station to a new pastry station on a Wednesday. The chain's cold-station ticket time "improves" by 22% the next week, and the owner asks whether the new kitchen training worked.
A firmware bug makes some kitchen screens send each bump event twice. Ticket counts per station rise about 8% for the affected locations, while orders and sales stay flat.

templates.title: Seller risk review — signals from aggregates, a given score, payment holds and an audit trail
templates.subtopic: point-in-time signals, case management, reproducible decisions

sections.scenario: A payments product serves about {{sellers}} active sellers. A risk team reviews sellers whose activity looks unusual, so that payments that are likely to be refunded or reversed do not leave the seller's balance before anyone has looked. Another team owns a risk score: you are given a service that returns a score and a score version for a seller and a set of input signals. Your system computes those signals from aggregates of the seller's own activity (for example volume compared with the seller's own history, refund and reversal rates, the mix of in-person and keyed-in payments), routes sellers to review, applies holds when a reviewer decides on one, and keeps the record. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), a hold delays part or all of a seller's deposits until a review is complete; it never changes what the seller has earned. {{reviewers}} reviewers work the queue, and the target is a decision within {{review_hours}} hours of a case opening.
sections.problem: Design the system: signal computation from aggregates (with the time each value was true), how the given score and a set of written rules open cases, the case and review workflow, how holds are applied and released, what the seller is told and when, and the audit trail. Show how, years later, anyone with the right access can reproduce exactly what the reviewer saw and why the decision was made. Say how you would measure whether reviews are timely and consistent, and whether holds fall unevenly on particular kinds of sellers. You do not design the score itself, and how someone might try to avoid these controls is out of scope.
sections.constraints: No hold is placed without a reviewer's decision, except a short automatic hold that a written rule allows and that a reviewer must confirm or release within {{review_hours}} hours. Every case, signal snapshot, score and version, rule version, decision, reason and message to the seller is kept for {{audit_years}} years (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Reviewers see only what a case needs; analysts outside the risk team see aggregates only. The system draws no legal conclusion and no judgement about a person's creditworthiness; it records what was observed and what was decided.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, periods and rates are hypothetical. Payment, refund and reversal events arrive from the payments platform within minutes; the balance and deposit systems are given and accept a hold or release instruction with a reason code. Signals are computed hourly; the score service answers in under 200 ms.
sections.criteria: Signals computed from aggregates with validity intervals (point-in-time correct) and versioned code; the given score called with its version recorded; cases as append-only state machines; a decision record that freezes signal values, score and version, rule version, reviewer, reason codes and messages, kept for {{audit_years}} years; holds applied and released through the deposit system with acknowledgement and reconciliation (every decided case has a matching hold state); queue design and capacity reasoning against {{reviewers}} reviewers and the {{review_hours}}-hour target, with safe introduction of new score versions (shadow scoring, capped case volume); least-privilege access for reviewers and aggregates for analysts; fairness and consistency measured from aggregates of outcomes (release rate, loss rate, time held) by category and region; stays general about risk signals, gives no detail that would help someone avoid a control, and draws no legal or credit conclusions; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a reviewer see a seller's individual customers' details?
clarifications.a: Only what the case needs, such as amounts, times and payment types for the flagged activity. Say how you enforce that.

clarifications.q: What does the seller see?
clarifications.a: That part of their deposits is held for review, roughly how long it usually takes, and what information could help. They do not see the score or the rules.

clarifications.q: Does a new score version apply to open cases?
clarifications.a: Your call. Existing decisions must stay explainable by the version that informed them.

clarifications.q: Can a seller appeal?
clarifications.a: Yes. An appeal reopens the case with a different reviewer, and the outcome is recorded alongside the original.

clarifications.q: Are signals ever corrected after the fact?
clarifications.a: Yes, when a bug is found. Decide what that means for decisions already made.

hints: A decision is reproducible only if the inputs are frozen at decision time: store a snapshot of the signal values, the score and its version, and the rule version on the case, not a pointer to tables that will be recomputed.
Treat the case as the unit of work: a state machine (opened, assigned, decided, appealed, closed) with every transition an append-only event carrying who and why.
Measure the queue the way a seller experiences it: time from case open to decision and from hold to release, by percentile, not only cases closed per day.
followups: Walk through one seller: an unusual week, a case opens, a reviewer places a partial hold, the seller sends information, the hold is released. Which records exist at the end?
How do you compute signals so that a value used three months ago can be shown exactly as it was, even after the signal job is fixed and rerun?
The score team ships a new version that would open twice as many cases. How do you introduce it without flooding the queue or changing past decisions?
How would you show, from aggregates, whether holds fall more often on certain business categories or regions than their outcomes justify, and what would you do with the answer?
A bug inflated one signal for a month. How do you find every decision it may have influenced, and what happens to those sellers?

rules.ask: A rule places automatic holds on 3,000 sellers in an hour, and reviewers can confirm or release about 200 an hour. What does a seller in that queue experience, and what stops this from happening again?
You rerun the signal job with a fix. A seller asks why they were held in March. Which numbers does the reviewer show them, the old ones or the corrected ones?
Where exactly is the value the reviewer saw stored, and what stops a later job from overwriting it?
Most held sellers are released with no loss. Is that a failing system, a cautious one, or a working one? What measure would tell you?
An analyst wants per-seller hold histories to study reviewer consistency. What do you give them?

incidents: A new score version goes live on a Monday and cases triple overnight. Within the week the oldest open case passes {{review_hours}} hours; most of the new cases are restaurants in one region whose volume rose legitimately after a holiday weekend.

A seller who was held four months ago asks for an explanation. The signal tables have since been recomputed after a bug fix, and the refund rate in today's table differs from the one the reviewer saw.
A change to the signal job counts each refund once per location for sellers with several locations, so their refund rates double for 11 days before anyone notices.
A release instruction to the deposit system fails silently for 2% of decided cases; those sellers' holds stay on for days after reviewers released them.

templates.title: Offline-capable point of sale — device-stored payments and orders, sync on reconnect, catalogue conflicts and late analytics
templates.subtopic: store-and-forward, conflict rules, watermarks and restated reports

sections.scenario: A point-of-sale app runs on about {{devices}} phones, tablets and registers, with up to {{devices_per_location}} devices at a location. When the device cannot reach the internet, the seller can keep taking card payments in offline mode: under this exercise's rule (check current docs), each offline payment is stored encrypted on the device and must be forwarded for authorisation within {{offline_hours}} hours of being taken, or it expires and cannot be processed; a payment declined when it is forwarded is the seller's loss; and a seller may set a per-payment limit for offline payments of up to {{offline_cap}}. Orders, items sold, discounts and stock decrements are also recorded on the device. Meanwhile the seller, or a colleague on another device, may change prices, items and stock counts in the online dashboard.
sections.problem: Design the device-side store, the sync protocol, the conflict rules for the catalogue and stock, and the analytics. Cover: how payments and orders are identified on the device so that forwarding twice never charges twice and never counts twice; the order in which a reconnecting device sends its backlog; what wins when the dashboard and an offline device both changed the same item, price or stock count; what the seller is shown about payments not yet forwarded and payments declined after forwarding; and how daily sales reports handle data that arrives up to {{offline_hours}} hours late.
sections.constraints: Card data stays encrypted on the device as the payment-industry rules require and never enters analytics. A device may be offline for minutes or for days. Payments must be forwarded in a bounded time after reconnecting even when thousands of devices reconnect together. Reports for a day may change after the day ends, but every change must be explainable, and the seller's sales summary must agree with what eventually settles.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, limits and periods are hypothetical. Each device has a stable device id and a monotonically increasing local sequence number. The payment authorisation service and the catalogue service are given; you design how the device and the data platform use them.
sections.criteria: Device-generated ids for payments and orders with server writes keyed by them, so forwarding and backlog retries are safe; per-device sequence numbers and an ordered, rate-controlled forwarding queue that drains within {{offline_hours}} hours and smooths a mass reconnection (jittered back-off, priority by time left before expiry); offline payments as explicit states (stored, forwarded, authorised, declined, expired) shown to the seller, with the {{offline_cap}} limit enforced on the device; conflict rules stated per field (sale price is what was charged; stock as merged signed changes with negative counts surfaced; catalogue edits versioned so reports know which price was current); card data encrypted on the device and absent from analytics; daily reports with per-device watermarks, provisional and final states and visible restatements; reconciliation of the sales summary with what authorised and settled; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can the device check stock with the server before selling offline?
clarifications.a: No. Offline, it only knows its last synced catalogue and its own sales.

clarifications.q: Which price is right if the dashboard changed it while the device was offline?
clarifications.a: The price the customer was charged is the sale price. Decide what the catalogue and the reports show.

clarifications.q: Do declined offline payments disappear from sales?
clarifications.a: Not silently. The seller must see them, and the reports must say what happened.

clarifications.q: Does an expired offline payment ever reach the payments platform?
clarifications.a: Not under this exercise's rule. It exists only on the device and in whatever the device reports about it.

clarifications.q: How late can an order event be?
clarifications.a: For a device that reconnects within the limit, up to {{offline_hours}} hours; orders without card payments can be later still.

hints: Create every payment and order id on the device, before anything is sent, and make every server-side write keyed by that id; then retrying a whole backlog is harmless.
Treat a stock count as a set of signed changes from many devices rather than a value to overwrite; changes merge, overwrites lose sales.
A daily report needs a watermark per device and a status per day (provisional, final); know how many devices still owe data for a day before calling it final.
followups: Walk through a device that goes offline at 11:00, takes 40 card payments, and reconnects at 17:00 after the price of one item changed in the dashboard at 13:00.
Two offline devices at one location each sell the last three units of an item. What stock does the dashboard show after both reconnect, and what does the seller see?
A regional outage reconnects tens of thousands of devices within ten minutes. How do you forward their payments quickly without overwhelming authorisation?
How do you decide when a day's sales report is final, and how are later corrections shown to the seller?
A device is lost with stored payments on it. What does the seller see, and what can be recovered?

rules.ask: The dashboard sets stock to 20 at 12:00; an offline device sold 5 at 11:30 and syncs at 13:00. What does last-write-wins leave, and is it right?
Merged decrements leave the count at −3 after two devices both sold the last units. What does the seller see, and who fixes it?
A device retries its backlog after a timeout, but the first attempt had in fact succeeded for half the payments. Walk through what the server does with each payment.
A device that owes Tuesday's data never reconnects. When does Tuesday become final, and what does the report say about that device?
Support wants to see the stored offline payments on a seller's lost tablet to help them. What can support see, and what can it never see?

incidents: A regional internet outage takes about 9,000 locations offline for six hours on a Saturday. When it ends, roughly 1.4 million stored payments are forwarded within 20 minutes, authorisation latency climbs to 9 seconds, and some devices time out and resend.

A tablet left in a drawer reconnects three hours after the {{offline_hours}}-hour limit has passed for its first offline payment. Its 60 oldest stored payments have expired; the seller's sales summary for that day still includes them.
A seller changes an item's price at 13:00; a device offline since 11:00 sells it 80 times at the old price and syncs at 17:00. The item's revenue per unit in the report is wrong for both prices.

Two registers at a busy location sold the same last units offline; after reconnecting, the dashboard shows −12 units for a best-selling item and the online store accepts orders against the next delivery that has not arrived.

templates.title: Deposits and instant transfers — schedules, cut-offs, measured arrival times and what sellers are shown
templates.subtopic: business calendars, rail status, honest arrival estimates

sections.scenario: About {{sellers}} sellers in {{countries}} countries receive their card sales as deposits to a linked bank account. Under this exercise's rules (check current docs): sales up to a daily cut-off in the seller's time zone are paid out in a standard deposit sent the next business day, where business days follow each country's bank holidays; a seller can instead request an instant transfer of their available balance at any time for a fee of {{fee}} of the amount, rounded once to the nearest cent with halves rounded up, with a minimum fee of 25 cents; and instant transfers are limited to {{daily_limit}} per seller per day. Standard deposits travel over bank batch networks that confirm days later or not at all; instant transfers travel over card-network or real-time rails that answer in seconds, though the money can still be returned. Sellers want to know when the money will arrive and whether it did.
sections.problem: Design the scheduling and status system and its analytics: computing each seller's next deposit (amount, send date, expected arrival) from their balance, cut-off and calendar; the instant transfer request path (eligibility against balance and limits, fee, submission, status); a single status model for both kinds of movement across rails; how arrival time is measured when banks confirm late or never; and what sellers are shown before, during and after a deposit, including returns to a closed bank account. The seller's balance itself is a given service you call; do not design it.
sections.constraints: Money is integer cents everywhere; the fee is computed once, by the stated rule, and shown before the seller confirms. An instant transfer request must never send money twice, even when the seller taps twice or the rail times out. Holiday calendars change and are sometimes wrong. The estimated arrival shown to sellers must be honest: if the estimate is missed for more than a small share of deposits on a rail, the estimate shown must change.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, fees, limits and timings are hypothetical. The balance service answers "available to transfer" and accepts a debit with a reference. Each rail's partner sends status events or files, on its own schedule, with its own codes.
sections.criteria: Scheduling from cut-offs in the seller's time zone and versioned per-country business calendars, recording the calendar version used; instant transfers with a client-generated request id, a single debit reference to the balance service, rail submission with an at-most-once guarantee and a status query before any resend; fee in integer cents by the stated rule (half up, minimum, computed once and shown before confirmation) and {{daily_limit}} enforced per seller per day in a stated time zone; one status model across rails mapping partner codes and keeping originals; arrival-time metrics that distinguish confirmed, inferred (no return within N days) and returned, per rail, bank and country; seller-facing estimates driven by measured arrival distributions and updated when missed; returns handled with notices and bank-detail fixes; eligibility limited to product limits with no credit or legal conclusions; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Whose time zone is the cut-off in?
clarifications.a: The seller's business location's, under this exercise's rule. A seller with locations in two zones uses the account's primary location.

clarifications.q: What is "eligible" for an instant transfer?
clarifications.a: Only product limits: available balance, a linked eligible card or account, and the daily limit. Nothing about the seller as a person, and no credit judgement.

clarifications.q: How do we know a standard deposit arrived?
clarifications.a: Often we do not. Some banks confirm; most stay silent unless the deposit is returned. Decide what "arrived" means for the metric.

clarifications.q: Can a seller cancel an instant transfer?
clarifications.a: Not once submitted to the rail.

clarifications.q: What happens to a returned deposit?
clarifications.a: The money comes back to the balance after some days, and the seller must be told and asked to fix their bank details.

hints: One status model for every movement (scheduled, submitted, sent, confirmed, returned, failed), with rail-specific codes mapped onto it and the original codes kept.
A business-day calendar is data with versions and owners, not code; schedule computation reads the version in force and records which one it used.
Arrival time without confirmations is an estimate: measure it where confirmations exist, use returns as the negative signal elsewhere, and label which is which.
followups: Walk through a seller in a country with a bank holiday on Monday: sales on Friday evening, Saturday and Sunday. When is each deposit sent, and what arrival date is shown?
A seller requests a $1,333.33 instant transfer. Compute the fee under this exercise's rule and show every number the seller sees.
The rail times out on an instant transfer and the seller taps "try again". What does the system do, and what does the seller see in the meantime?
How do you compute and publish the share of deposits that arrived by the date shown, per rail and country, when most banks never confirm?
A country's holiday calendar was missing a date last month. How do you find every seller who was shown a wrong date, and what do you tell them?

rules.ask: The nightly scheduling run fails halfway through on the night before a holiday weekend. Which sellers have a deposit, which do not, and how do you finish without paying anyone twice?
The rail answered after your timeout, and the transfer succeeded. Your retry is already on its way. What stops the second one?
For one bank, a quarter of deposits arrive a day later than shown. How would you find out, and what do you change on the seller's screen?
Show me the exact cents of the fee on $1,333.33 and on $10.00, and the line of code that does the rounding.
A government announces a one-off bank holiday four days ahead. Who updates the calendar, and what happens to deposits already scheduled for that day?

incidents: A bank holiday in one of the {{countries}} countries is missing from the calendar. About 40,000 sellers are shown Monday as the arrival date for deposits that arrive on Tuesday, and support contacts triple that morning.
One rail partner's status file is two days late. The arrival-time dashboard shows instant transfers on that rail taking 50 hours, and an alert fires to every seller with a pending transfer.
On the last evening of the month instant transfer requests rise sixfold; 10% of rail calls time out, sellers tap again, and a handful of sellers report two transfers where they asked for one.

A change to the fee code rounds every fee down instead of half up. Over a week, 2.3 million instant transfers are charged a cent less than the {{fee}} rule says, and the daily fee report no longer matches the transfers.

templates.title: Card reader and register fleet telemetry with seller-facing device health
templates.subtopic: relayed and intermittent uploads, fleet health by model and version, seller alerts

sections.scenario: Sellers use about {{devices}} payment devices across {{models}} hardware models: card readers that pair over Bluetooth with the seller's phone or tablet and have no internet connection of their own, and registers and terminals that connect directly over Wi-Fi, Ethernet or a mobile network. Each device can report battery level and charging state, signal strength and connection drops, its firmware and app versions, and counts of card-read errors by type. A register reports every {{interval}} while switched on; a reader reports only through the app on a paired device, and only while that app is running. Sellers want a device health page (which readers need charging, which are out of date, which keep disconnecting) and timely alerts; the hardware and firmware teams want fleet health by model and version.
sections.problem: Design the telemetry system: what devices send and how often, the relay path for readers, ingestion, deduplication and ordering, the current-state store behind the seller's device health page, the alerting rules and their limits, and the fleet analytics by model, firmware version and age. Define the main fleet measures precisely (for example a model's card-read error rate, a battery's health over time, the share of devices on the current firmware), and say how a device that has not reported is treated in each.
sections.constraints: Telemetry never contains card numbers, customer data or anything typed on the device; a seller's devices are identified by serial number and the seller's location, never by a customer. Raw telemetry is kept {{retention_days}} days; daily aggregates by model and version are kept longer. A seller is not sent more than one alert per device per day for the same condition. The device health page must reflect a report within a minute of it arriving.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, intervals and periods are hypothetical. Each device has a serial number, a model and a factory date. Readers buffer a limited number of reports in memory and upload them in a batch when the app connects; device clocks drift and can reset when the battery fully drains.
sections.criteria: A telemetry contract with typed fields and no card or customer data; readers relayed through the paired app with buffered batches, registers reporting every {{interval}}; deduplication on (serial, sequence) and both device and receive times kept, with clock-reset detection; a current-state store per device feeding the seller's page within a minute, with "not reporting" as an explicit state; alert rules with debouncing, minimum durations, per-device daily caps and plausibility checks per model; fleet measures defined per device-day (or with capped weights) by model, firmware and age, with confidence for small firmware cohorts and awareness of upload delay; {{retention_days}}-day raw retention with longer-lived aggregates designed for the questions the hardware team will ask; least-privilege access to per-device data; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a reader be paired with more than one phone?
clarifications.a: Yes, one at a time; a reader moves between a seller's devices during the day.

clarifications.q: What counts as an active device?
clarifications.a: You define it, and it must not count a reader twice because it reported through two phones.

clarifications.q: May we read the device's location?
clarifications.a: Only the seller's registered location; no device positioning.

clarifications.q: Can the firmware team ask for raw reports from one device?
clarifications.a: For a support case with the seller's consent, yes; otherwise only aggregates.

hints: Key every report by (serial number, device sequence number) so the same report relayed twice, or uploaded again after a crash, is counted once.
Keep two clocks per report: the device's and the server's receive time. Trust the server's for "last seen" and use the device's only within checked bounds.
Absence is a state: "no report for N intervals" must be distinguished from "reported and healthy" in both the seller's page and the fleet measures.
followups: Walk through one reader across a day: paired to two phones, unpaired overnight, then reporting a low battery. What does the seller's page show at each point?
Define the card-read error rate per model and firmware version so that a seller who uses one reader all day does not dominate it.
A firmware version is installed on 10% of one model's readers. How quickly can your system say whether its error rate is worse, and with what confidence?
How do you keep low-battery alerts useful rather than noisy across {{devices}} devices?
Six months later the hardware team asks how battery health declines with age per model. What have you kept that answers it within {{retention_days}} days of raw data?

rules.ask: Readers only report while the seller's app is open. What does your stream see overnight, and what does the seller's page show at 8 a.m. before the shop opens?
A reader's battery fully drains and its clock resets to 1 January 2000. Where do its next reports land, and how do you find them?
One model reports 0% battery while in deep sleep. How many alerts go out overnight, and what in your design stops them?
One reader at a busy food stall makes 4,000 reads a day; most readers make 30. Whose experience does your error rate describe?
A support case needs one reader's raw reports. Who can see them, for how long, and what is logged about that access?

incidents: A firmware version reaches 10% of one model's readers and card-read errors rise for those sellers, but the fleet dashboard shows nothing for six hours because readers upload only when the seller's app is open, and most were closed overnight.
One reader model reports 0% battery while in deep sleep. Overnight, about 200,000 "charge your reader" alerts are queued for sellers whose readers are fine.
Readers whose batteries fully drained reset their clocks to 1 January 2000; their next reports land in partitions dated 2000, and the share of the fleet on the current firmware drops by four points.
A bug in the phone app re-uploads the last batch of reader reports at every app launch; daily card reads per reader for one of the {{models}} models double while payment counts stay flat.

templates.title: A seller publicly challenges a payment hold your data helped inform
templates.subtopic: verification, privacy, correction, decision rights

finding: the signals were correct and the review followed the written process, but the review queue was days behind
one signal your team computes was inflated by a recent change that double-counted refunds for sellers with several locations
the signals were correct, but the message the seller received gave no idea of how long the review would take
reach: a local news site picks it up
it is shared widely by other sellers
a seller association asks for a meeting about holds in general

sections.scenario: Your team computes the aggregate signals that, together with a score another team provides, open review cases for sellers on a payments platform. Reviewers in a separate risk operations team decide on holds; under this exercise's rule a hold delays part of a seller's deposits until the review is complete. A small-business owner posts that their deposits have been held for {{days}} days with no explanation, and {{reach}}. Communications and risk operations ask your team, the same morning, whether the data was right. After two hours of checking you believe {{finding}}.
sections.problem: What do you do over the first day and the following weeks? Cover how you confirm what you believe before you report it, what you tell risk operations and communications and how fast, what you do about other sellers who may be affected, what you change in your own team's systems and practices, and what you must not do. Then tell me about a real time data you owned informed a decision that someone challenged, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not decide holds and you do not speak publicly for the company. Nothing about an individual seller's account may be shared outside the people who need it for the case. The review draws no legal conclusion and no judgement of the seller's creditworthiness. Your team is midway through a committed project.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Verifies before reporting (the frozen case record, the signal values and their code version, a recomputation, the queue and message history) and reports early with stated confidence; clear separation of data correctness, process and treatment, owning the first; protects the seller's information and respects that risk operations decides and communications speaks; finds every case the same cause could have touched and gives decision-makers what they need to re-review promptly; blameless handling inside the team with a specific prevention (tests on multi-location sellers, distribution monitors, frozen snapshots, queue-age alerts, better messages); no legal or credit conclusions; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can you see the case record?
clarifications.a: Yes, the frozen record of what the reviewer saw, through the access your role has for incidents.

clarifications.q: Who talks to the seller?
clarifications.a: Risk operations and support; communications handles anything public.

clarifications.q: Is the seller right?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet whether the hold itself was justified. You only know about the data and the process.

clarifications.q: Does anyone want a name for the mistake?
clarifications.a: Someone asks which engineer made the change. How you answer is part of the question.

hints: Separate three questions: was the data right, was the process followed, was the seller treated well. Your team owns the first and influences the others.
Report what you know with its confidence and what you will know by when, rather than waiting for certainty.
Look for every other case the same cause could have touched before anyone asks.
followups: What exactly do you check in the first two hours, and how do you decide you are confident enough to report?
What do you write to risk operations and communications, and what do you leave out?
How do you find other sellers affected by the same cause, and what should happen to their cases?
Communications asks for a sentence they can say publicly about the data. What do you give them?
In your real example, what changed in how your team builds or checks the data afterwards?

rules.ask: You are not the company's spokesperson. Why is answering the seller yourself a problem, even with good intentions?
A senior leader asks which engineer made the change. What do you say, and what do you do next with your team?
Reverting the change fixes new signals. What about the decisions already made with the inflated values?
You do not decide holds. What do you give the people who do, so they can decide quickly and well?
Communications wants the seller's case details to prepare a statement. What do they get from you?

templates.title: A team that never writes anything down
templates.subtopic: lightweight written decisions, runbooks, knowledge spread

system: the pipeline behind sellers' daily sales summaries
the service that computes instalment schedules for purchases
the reader and register telemetry pipeline
trigger: an outage lasted five hours because the only person who knew the recovery steps was on a flight
a new engineer took four months to make a change on their own
an auditor asked why a rounding rule was chosen, and nobody could say

sections.scenario: You have just become the technical lead of a team of {{team_size}} engineers that owns {{system}}. The team is fast and proud of it. Decisions are made in chat threads and calls; there are no design documents, the runbooks are a few lines in a wiki page last edited two years ago, and the people who have been there longest hold most of the knowledge. Last month {{trigger}}. When you raise documentation, people say it goes stale, slows them down and nobody reads it.
sections.problem: How would you change this? Cover what you would write first and why, what the team writes from now on and in what form, how you keep it short and current, how you get the longest-serving engineers to take part rather than resent it, and how you would know in six months that it is working. Then tell me about a real time you changed how a team records decisions or knowledge, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The team's delivery commitments for the quarter stand. You cannot hire a technical writer. You are not anyone's manager.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Starts from the felt cost ({{trigger}}) and writes that first, often personally; small formats attached to existing work (decision records linked from pull requests, runbooks tested in drills, onboarding paths built by the newest engineer); engages the longest-serving engineers by reducing their interruptions and giving them authorship, not by mandate; keeps documents current through ownership and review dates, and accepts deleting what nobody uses; decisions that must be explained later (rounding, retention) recorded with context and alternatives; success measured in recovery time, ramp time and expert interruptions; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does the team's manager support this?
clarifications.a: Yes, but expects you to lead it and does not want velocity to drop noticeably.

clarifications.q: Is there a company template for design documents?
clarifications.a: There is one, eleven pages long, which is part of why the team avoids it.

clarifications.q: Who knows the most?
clarifications.a: Two engineers who built most of the system; both are busy and are asked everything.

clarifications.q: Are there compliance needs?
clarifications.a: Some decisions, such as rounding and retention rules, must be explainable later to people outside the team.

hints: Start where the cost of not writing was felt: the incident, the slow ramp or the unanswered question, and write that first.
Make the smallest useful format the default (a half-page decision record, a runbook entry tested in a drill) and attach it to work that already happens, such as code review.
Measure the effect in things the team cares about: time to recover, time for a new engineer's first change, questions sent to the two experts.
followups: What are the first three documents you write or get written, and who writes each?
One of the two experts says writing things down is a waste of their time. What do you do?
Six months in, half the decision records are out of date. Is that a failure? What do you change?
How do you make sure the rounding rule and retention rule decisions survive the people who made them?
In your real example, what did you stop asking people to write, and why?

rules.ask: The team already avoids an eleven-page template. Why will yours be different, and what is the smallest version that still works?
The last wiki went stale in a year. What keeps these pages current without you policing them?
Show me what one entry for the rounding rule would say, in five lines.
Who has followed that runbook without its author in the room, and what changed after they did?
What did you personally write or change first?

templates.title: Supporting a teammate going through a hard time during a critical launch
templates.subtopic: care with privacy, redistributing work, honest launch risk

launch: instant transfers for sellers in a new country
offline payments on a new card reader model
a new instalment option at checkout
role: a peer on the same team

sections.scenario: Your team is {{weeks}} weeks from launching {{launch}}, with a date announced to sellers. You are {{role}}. A teammate who owns a critical part of the launch, the reconciliation checks that prove the numbers sellers see are right, has missed two standups, their work has slowed sharply, and in a one-to-one they tell you, briefly, that something difficult is happening in their life. They do not offer details, and they say they do not want the team to know.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover what you say and do in that conversation, what you do in the following days, how you handle their part of the launch without exposing what they told you, who else you involve and what you tell them, and how you decide whether the launch date is still safe. Then tell me about a real time you supported someone through a hard period while work had to continue, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Their privacy is theirs; you may not share what they told you without their agreement. The reconciliation checks must exist before launch. You are not a counsellor, and company support resources exist.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Leads the first conversation with care: listens, does not probe, asks what would help and what may be shared, points to company support and, where relevant, time-off options through the right channel; protects their privacy in every later conversation; re-plans the work openly on the work's merits (pairing, moving parts of the reconciliation checks, cutting scope that is not needed for launch) with the teammate's agreement; involves the manager or people team in the way that fits being {{role}}; decides the date on evidence about the work and escalates early if the checks that prove sellers' numbers are at risk; follows up over weeks without turning care into monitoring; real example with what they did personally and what they learned, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does the teammate want time off?
clarifications.a: They have not said. They seem to want to keep working but cannot work as before right now.

clarifications.q: Can someone else build the reconciliation checks?
clarifications.a: One other engineer could, slowly, with the teammate's help or notes.

clarifications.q: Does your manager know?
clarifications.a: Not yet. If you are the manager, your own manager does not.

clarifications.q: Is the date negotiable?
clarifications.a: It has been announced to sellers; moving it is possible but costly and visible.

hints: In the conversation, listen, ask what would help and what they want shared, and point to the support available; do not ask for details they did not offer.
Separate the person from the plan: agree with them what changes in their work, then re-plan the launch with the team using only what they agreed to share.
Decide the launch question on the work, not on the person: what must exist, who can build it, and how much time remains.
followups: What do you say in the first conversation, and what do you avoid saying?
The team asks why the work moved. What do you say?
Two weeks before launch, the reconciliation checks are still not done. What do you recommend, and to whom?
If you are not their manager, what is your role and what is not, and when do you involve the manager?
In your real example, what would you do differently?

rules.ask: When do you involve those resources, and what do you tell the teammate before you do?
What exactly do you say to the team, and has your teammate agreed to it?
Who decides whether the date moves, and what evidence do you bring them?
How do you move the work without signalling to the team that something is wrong with your teammate?
How often, and how do you avoid making each check-in feel like a status report?

templates.title: Learning a new domain fast after joining a payments team
templates.subtopic: domain learning, verifying understanding, early contribution without risk

first_task: own the dashboard that tells sellers when their deposits will arrive
explain why sellers' sales summaries and their deposits differ by a few cents on some days
review a design for forwarding payments taken in offline mode

sections.scenario: You have joined a data team in a payments business as a senior engineer, coming from {{background}}. Words such as authorisation, capture, settlement, deposit, return, interchange, minor units and cut-off are used in every meeting, and most of the team has worked with payments for years. Your manager asks you to {{first_task}}, with a first result expected in {{weeks}} weeks.
sections.problem: How would you get up to speed? Cover what you learn first and how, how you check that what you think you understand is right, who you learn from and how you avoid becoming a burden, how you deliver something useful within {{weeks}} weeks without making a mistake that costs sellers money, and what you bring from your previous domain. Then tell me about a real time you had to learn a new domain quickly, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Money is handled in integer minor units, and a mistake in what sellers are shown is visible to them at once. Your teammates are busy with their own commitments.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical. Payment terms are used in their general industry sense.
sections.criteria: A deliberate learning plan: one payment traced end to end in systems and data, a personal glossary and diagrams checked by experts, predictions tested against real (aggregated or test) data; respectful use of experts' time (corrections of written understanding, batched questions, learning from support and finance as well as engineers); an early contribution that is useful and safe (read-only analysis, tests, documentation fixes, a reviewed change behind checks) rather than a risky change to what sellers see; correct handling of money in minor units and awareness of cut-offs and settlement timing; honest about what transferred from the previous domain and what misled; real example with how they knew they understood, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is there documentation?
clarifications.a: Some, of uneven quality, and parts of it describe how things worked two years ago.

clarifications.q: Who is the expert?
clarifications.a: One engineer knows deposits deeply and is often in meetings; finance and support also know a lot.

clarifications.q: Can you look at real data?
clarifications.a: Yes, aggregated data and test accounts, with the usual access controls.

clarifications.q: Is anyone checking your work?
clarifications.a: Code review, yes. Nobody will check your understanding unless you ask.

hints: Follow one payment end to end through the systems and the data, from tap to deposit, and write down what you see at each step.
Turn understanding into predictions you can check: if a sale happens at 23:55 on a Friday, which deposit includes it, and when does it arrive?
Ask experts to correct something you wrote rather than to explain from scratch; it costs them less and finds your gaps faster.
followups: What do you do in your first week, day by day?
Your write-up of how deposits work has an error that an expert spots. How did you find out, and what do you change in how you learn?
What could you deliver within the first {{weeks}} weeks that helps, and what would you deliberately not touch yet?
What from {{background}} turned out to be useful, and what was misleading?
In your real example, how did you know you had understood the domain well enough?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for payments for sellers and people, with offline-capable devices
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, minor units, late device data and seller-visible totals

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: money in integer minor units end to end, with one stated rounding step
payments taken offline and forwarded days later, counted once and in the right day
the same totals in a seller's sales report and in their deposits
people's and customers' data shown only in aggregates outside a seller's own view
scale: tens of millions of people sending money to each other

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for point-of-sale and peer-to-peer payments, at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The payments setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example integer minor units in every schema with rounding at one named step; device-generated payment ids, per-device watermarks and dated restatements; one source of settled amounts feeding both the sales report and the deposit with a daily reconciliation; aggregates with minimum group sizes and per-seller views scoped to the seller); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a payments system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.

What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?
